name: Classic-Style Test 2
source: Original questions written for LSAT Trainer in the style and difficulty of recent LSATs. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: A survey of 600 adults found that those who regularly sing in a choir reported feeling lonely far less often than did those who do not sing in any group. This difference held for younger and older respondents alike. Clearly, then, joining a choir is an effective way for a person to reduce loneliness.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: draws a general conclusion about adults from a survey that included only some of the adults in the population
takes for granted that singing in a choir is the only effective way for a person to reduce loneliness
overlooks the possibility that people who seldom feel lonely are more inclined than others to join a choir
fails to consider that some people who sing in a choir may nonetheless feel lonely on occasion
confuses how often people feel lonely with how intensely they feel lonely when they do
questions.explanation: The survey shows only a correlation between choir singing and low loneliness, yet the argument concludes that joining a choir reduces loneliness. It ignores reversed causation: people who are already seldom lonely may be the ones who join choirs, which is (C). (A) is tempting because the evidence is a survey, but every survey covers only some of a population, and nothing suggests this one is unrepresentative. (B) and (D) attribute claims the argument never makes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Joining a choir is an effective way for a person to reduce loneliness.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In a survey of 600 adults, regular choir singers reported feeling lonely far less often than people who sing in no group, at every age.

breakdown.analysis: So choir singers are less lonely. Does that mean the choir made them that way? Maybe the arrow runs backwards: people who are already social and rarely lonely are the ones who sign up for a choir, while lonely people avoid group activities in the first place. It's like noticing that people at parties are less lonely and concluding parties cure loneliness. Prephrase: the argument ignores that low loneliness might lead to choir membership, not the other way around.

choices.note: Tempting because it's a survey, but every survey covers only some of a population. Nothing suggests this sample of 600 is unrepresentative, and the age detail suggests it's fairly broad. The problem is the causal leap, not the sample.
choices.example: Example of flaw: We asked 20 people at a jazz club about their favorite music, so jazz must be the most popular genre in the country.

choices.note: The argument says a choir is "an effective way," not the only way. It never rules out other cures for loneliness.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Exercise lowers stress, so anyone who wants less stress has no choice but to exercise.

choices.note: CORRECT. Reversed causation. If people who are seldom lonely are more likely to join choirs, choir singers would report less loneliness even if singing did nothing at all for loneliness.
The argument doesn't claim choir members are never lonely. "Far less often" already allows some loneliness.
choices.example: Example of flaw: This medicine reduces headaches, so no one who takes it will ever get a headache again.

choices.note: The argument never mixes up frequency and intensity. It talks only about how often, on both sides.
choices.example: Example of flaw: She cries less often than he does, so she must feel sadness less deeply.

questions.stimulus:
Kemal: The city's new limit on short-term rentals in residential neighborhoods will lower rents. Many apartments now rented to tourists will return to the long-term market, and that added supply will push rents down.

Rosa: Some apartments will indeed return to long-term tenants, but not enough of them to bring rents down. Most of the city's short-term rentals are spare rooms in owner-occupied houses, and their owners will simply stop renting them out.
questions.stem: Kemal and Rosa disagree over whether
choices: the limit on short-term rentals will bring about a reduction in the rents charged in the city
some apartments now rented to tourists will become available to long-term tenants as a result of the limit
most of the city's short-term rentals are spare rooms in houses whose owners live in them
the city acted wisely in adopting a limit on short-term rentals in its residential neighborhoods
owners of spare rooms will stop renting them out rather than offer them to long-term tenants
questions.explanation: Kemal says the limit will lower rents; Rosa says it will not return enough apartments to bring rents down, so they disagree over (A). (B) is the trap: Rosa's "will indeed" concedes Kemal's point, so they agree on it. (C) and (E) are Rosa's claims alone, since Kemal never mentions spare rooms, and neither speaker evaluates the policy, as (D) requires.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Kemal: The limit will lower rents because many tourist apartments will return to the long-term market.; Rosa: Some apartments will return, but not enough to bring rents down, because most short-term rentals are spare rooms whose owners will just stop renting.

breakdown.analysis: Find the claim one says yes to and the other says no to. Kemal: rents will go down. Rosa: no, not enough apartments come back. That's the split. Watch Rosa's "will indeed": it's a concession, so whatever follows it is something they agree on, not a disagreement. Lesson: to disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no.

choices.note: CORRECT. Kemal: the limit "will lower rents." Rosa: "not enough of them to bring rents down." Yes versus no on the same question.
Tempting, since it's the topic of the first sentences. But Rosa concedes it ("will indeed"). They agree here.
Rosa's claim alone. Kemal says nothing about spare rooms, so he takes no position.
Neither speaker says whether the city was right. They only predict the limit's effect on rents.
Rosa's prediction alone. Kemal never discusses what owners of spare rooms will do.

questions.stimulus: In the orchards of the Varrow Valley, the population of the native orange-banded bee has fallen sharply over the past decade, the same period during which growers there widely adopted a new fungicide. Although the fungicide's manufacturer reports that it was not designed to affect insects, the fungicide is most likely responsible for the bees' decline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: The new fungicide controls orchard fungi more effectively than did the products that growers used before it.
In valley orchards where the new fungicide has never been used, orange-banded bee numbers have held steady.
Orange-banded bees visit orchard blossoms less often than several other bee species in the valley do.
Over the past decade, a parasitic mite that attacks orange-banded bees has spread throughout the valley.
Some growers in the valley have recently begun planting wildflowers near their orchards to attract bees.
questions.explanation: The only evidence is timing: the bees declined while the fungicide spread. (B) adds a comparison group: where the fungicide was never used, the bees did not decline, which points to the fungicide rather than a valley-wide cause. (D) is on topic but names a rival cause, so it weakens; (A), (C), and (E) say nothing about what caused the decline.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new fungicide is most likely responsible for the orange-banded bees' decline.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The bee population fell sharply over the past decade, the same period in which growers widely adopted the fungicide.

breakdown.analysis: Two things happened at once. So what? Lots of things changed in the valley over ten years. To strengthen, show the decline tracks the fungicide: places without it, bees doing fine. It's like blaming the new office coffee for your headaches; you'd be surer if coworkers who skip the coffee aren't getting headaches. Prephrase: untreated orchards kept their bees.

choices.note: How well the fungicide kills fungi says nothing about whether it hurts bees. Irrelevant.
CORRECT. A control group. Where the fungicide was never used, bee numbers held steady. So whatever is hurting the bees is tied to treated orchards, not some valley-wide cause.
If anything, less blossom visiting means less exposure. It doesn't link the fungicide to the decline.
Weakens. A mite spreading over the same decade is a rival cause. On topic, wrong direction.
A recent response to the decline. It tells us nothing about what caused it.

questions.stimulus: Real estate agent: A house priced far below similar homes nearby is seldom the bargain it appears to be. Sellers rarely set a low price without a reason, and that reason is often a defect, such as a cracked foundation or a history of flooding, that an ordinary walkthrough will not reveal. Admittedly, some sellers simply need to sell quickly. But a buyer has no way of knowing which kind of seller he or she is dealing with.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the conclusion drawn in the real estate agent's argument?
choices: Sellers who set an unusually low price for a house usually do so because the house has a hidden defect.
Some sellers set a low price on a house only because they need to sell it quickly.
A buyer cannot tell whether a low price reflects a hidden defect or merely a seller's haste.
A house priced far below similar nearby homes is unlikely to be the bargain that it appears to be.
Buyers should have any unusually low-priced house professionally inspected before they make an offer on it.
questions.explanation: Everything after the first sentence supports it: sellers have reasons for low prices, the reason is often a hidden defect, and the possibility of a merely hasty seller is neutralized because buyers cannot tell the difference. So the conclusion is (D). (C) is the tempting choice, but it is the final premise that answers the concession, not the point being argued for; (A) overstates 'often' as 'usually', and (E) recommends something the agent never says.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: A house priced far below similar nearby homes is seldom the bargain it appears to be.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Sellers rarely set a low price without reason; that reason is often a hidden defect; some sellers just need to sell fast (concession), but buyers can't tell which kind of seller they're dealing with.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. Here it's the first sentence. Everything after supports it, including the concession-and-answer at the end: yes, some sellers are just in a hurry, but you can't tell them apart, so a cheap price is still a warning sign. Like saying "That too-good-to-be-true car on the lot probably has a problem. Sure, sometimes the owner just moved away, but you can't tell which it is."

choices.note: Overstates a premise. The agent says the reason is "often" a defect, not "usually." And even stated correctly, it's support, not the conclusion.
The concession. The agent admits it only to neutralize it. Not the main point.
Tempting. It's the final sentence, but it's there to answer the concession, which protects the main claim. It's a premise, not the point being argued.
CORRECT. Same as the first sentence: a house priced far below similar homes is seldom a real bargain. Every other sentence supports it.
The agent never recommends inspections. Plausible advice, but not in the argument.

questions.stimulus: The town of Merriton has two pharmacies, which charge nearly identical prices for prescription drugs and accept the same insurance plans. Yet Hollins Pharmacy, which is open only on weekdays, fills far more prescriptions each month than does Cardale Pharmacy, which is open seven days a week and stays open later each evening.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why Hollins Pharmacy fills more prescriptions than Cardale Pharmacy does?
choices: Hollins Pharmacy shares a building with the clinic where most Merriton residents see their doctors.
Most prescriptions in Merriton are filled on weekday afternoons, when both pharmacies are open.
Cardale Pharmacy employs more pharmacists than Hollins does and so can fill prescriptions more quickly.
Cardale Pharmacy also sells groceries and household goods, which draws many shoppers into the store.
Some Merriton residents have their prescriptions filled by mail-order services rather than at either pharmacy.
questions.explanation: We need some advantage of Hollins that outweighs Cardale's longer hours, given equal prices and insurance. (A) supplies one: patients leaving the clinic with a prescription can fill it in the same building. (B) is tempting, but it only cancels Cardale's advantage without giving Hollins one; (C) and (D) make the gap more puzzling, and (E) affects both pharmacies equally.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Two pharmacies charge about the same and take the same insurance; Cardale is open seven days and later each evening, but weekday-only Hollins fills far more prescriptions.

breakdown.analysis: Same prices, same insurance, Cardale has more hours, yet Hollins wins big. So Hollins must have some other edge. Location is a natural one: if Hollins is where people get prescriptions in the first place, they'll fill them there. It's like a coffee cart in a hospital lobby outselling a café down the street that's open longer. Prephrase: something draws customers to Hollins.

choices.note: CORRECT. Walk out of the doctor's office with a prescription, fill it downstairs. That's an advantage big enough to beat longer hours.
Tempting. It shows Cardale's extra hours don't matter much, but both stores are open then. It removes Cardale's edge without giving Hollins one, so we still don't know why Hollins wins.
More pharmacists and faster service should help Cardale. Deepens the puzzle.
More shoppers in Cardale should mean more chances to fill prescriptions there. Deepens the puzzle.
Mail order takes business from both pharmacies. It doesn't explain the gap between them.

questions.stimulus: At Quillon Software, an employee may work from home on a given day only if that employee's team lead has approved it in advance. Team leads approve such requests only from employees who have completed the company's security training. Moreover, an employee working from home may not access the customer database that day unless he or she uses the company's encrypted connection.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: Any Quillon employee who has completed the security training may work from home whenever he or she requests it.
Every Quillon employee who uses the company's encrypted connection on a given day is working from home that day.
Quillon's team leads approve most of the requests to work from home that they receive from trained employees.
A Quillon employee who uses the encrypted connection does not need a team lead's approval to work from home.
Any Quillon employee who works from home on a given day must have completed the company's security training.
questions.explanation: Working from home requires advance approval, and approval is given only to employees who have completed the training, so anyone working from home has completed it: (E). (A) reverses the chain, treating completed training as enough to work from home rather than as a requirement. (B) likewise reverses the encrypted-connection rule, (C) adds a frequency the rules never give, and (D) contradicts the first rule.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Work from home on a day → team lead approved in advance; 2. team lead approves → employee completed security training; 3. working from home AND accessing the customer database → uses encrypted connection.

breakdown.analysis: Chain the first two: work from home → approval → training. So anyone working from home has completed training. The third rule is a side branch about the database. Every rule gives requirements; none gives guarantees. Reversing an arrow is the classic wrong answer here.

choices.note: Reverses the chain. Training is required for approval; it doesn't guarantee approval, let alone working from home whenever you like.
Reverses the third rule. The encrypted connection is required for home database access; using it doesn't mean you're home. Office workers could use it too.
The rules say nothing about how many requests get approved. Unsupported.
Contradicts rule 1. Every work-from-home day needs a team lead's approval, encrypted connection or not.
CORRECT. Work from home → approved → trained. Straight down the chain.

questions.stimulus: Meteorologist: Our station's new forecasting model correctly predicted whether it would rain the next day on 88 percent of days last spring. The model we used before it was correct on only 74 percent of days during the previous spring. Both figures were checked against the same set of rain gauges. So the new model predicts next-day rain more accurately than the old one did.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the meteorologist's argument?
choices: The new model will be correct on at least 88 percent of days during the coming spring as well.
The old model was more accurate during the spring than it was during any other season of the year.
Next-day rain last spring was not substantially easier to predict than it had been during the previous spring.
No other forecasting model that is currently available to the station is any more accurate than the new model.
The new model requires less computing time to produce a forecast than the old model required.
questions.explanation: The models were tested in different springs, so the comparison works only if the two springs posed similar forecasting challenges. If last spring's weather was much easier to forecast, the higher score would not show that the model is better; that is (C). (A) is not required, because the conclusion concerns the models' accuracy so far, not next spring; (D) concerns other models, which the argument never compares.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new model predicts next-day rain more accurately than the old one did.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: New model correct on 88% of days last spring; old model correct on 74% of days the previous spring; same rain gauges for both.

breakdown.analysis: Same gauges, fine, but different springs. Is that a fair test? Only if the two springs were about equally hard to forecast. If last spring was sunny almost every day, any model would score well. Like comparing two students' scores on two different exams without knowing whether one exam was easier. We need an answer that says last spring wasn't the easy exam. Negation test on each choice.

choices.note: The conclusion is about how the models have performed, not a promise for next spring. Negated (it dips below 88% next year), the argument still stands.
choices.negation: The new model will not be correct on at least 88 percent of days next spring.

choices.note: Other seasons are irrelevant. Negated (the old model did better in fall), the spring comparison is unaffected.
choices.negation: The old model was not more accurate in spring than in every other season.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negated, last spring's rain was much easier to predict. Then the 88% vs. 74% gap could come from easier weather, not a better model. The comparison collapses, so it's required.
choices.negation: Next-day rain last spring was substantially easier to predict than it was during the previous spring.

choices.note: The argument compares only the new and old models. A better third model doesn't matter. Negation is harmless.
choices.negation: Some forecasting model available to the station is more accurate than the new model.

choices.note: Computing time has nothing to do with accuracy. Negation is harmless.
choices.negation: The new model does not require less computing time than the old model did.

questions.stimulus: Archaeologist: At the hilltop site of Tel Varo, we found grinding stones together with charred barley grains in a layer dated to about 9,000 years ago. Grinding stones were used to process grain into flour. So the people who lived at Tel Varo must already have been farming barley by that time, well before farming is usually thought to have reached the region.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the archaeologist's argument?
choices: Grinding stones found at several other sites in the region are older than those at Tel Varo.
The charred barley grains at Tel Varo were dated by a method that is considered highly reliable.
Wild barley grew abundantly near Tel Varo then, and people elsewhere ground wild grain long before farming began.
Later layers at Tel Varo contain clear evidence that barley was being cultivated near the site.
Barley is easier to grind into flour than most of the other cereal grains of the region.
questions.explanation: The evidence shows that people at Tel Varo ground barley, but the conclusion is that they farmed it. (C) shows that the evidence fits equally well with gathering and grinding wild barley, so it does not establish farming. (D) may look relevant because it mentions cultivation, but farming in later layers says nothing about whether farming had begun 9,000 years ago; (B) supports a premise.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The people at Tel Varo were already farming barley about 9,000 years ago.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Grinding stones and charred barley grains were found together in a 9,000-year-old layer; grinding stones were used to process grain.

breakdown.analysis: They ground barley. Does that mean they grew it? You can grind grain you gathered from the wild. It's like finding a fishing rod and a trout in a cabin and concluding the owner ran a fish farm. We need an answer that says the barley could have been wild.

choices.note: Older grinding stones elsewhere don't tell us whether Tel Varo's people farmed. Irrelevant to the grinding-vs-farming gap.
Reliable dating supports a premise. If anything, it strengthens.
CORRECT. Wild barley was abundant, and people elsewhere ground wild grain before farming existed. So stones plus barley fit gathering just as well as farming.
Tempting because it mentions cultivation. But later layers are later. Farming afterward doesn't show farming had started 9,000 years ago.
How easy barley is to grind doesn't tell us where it came from. Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Editor: A publisher should reissue an out-of-print book only if two conditions are met. First, the author, or the author's estate if the author has died, must consent to the reissue. Second, it must be possible to correct in the new edition any factual errors that have been discovered in the book since it first appeared.
questions.stem: The principle stated by the editor most helps to justify the reasoning in which one of the following arguments?
choices: Hollis Books should reissue Meera Dahl's first novel. Dahl has consented to the reissue, and no factual errors have been discovered in the novel since it first appeared.
Grayline Press should not reissue Owen Tarr's travel memoir. Tarr's estate favors a reissue, but the errors found in the memoir since it first appeared cannot be corrected.
Fenwick House should not reissue its 1970s cookbook, since the original edition sold poorly and there is little reason to expect that a new edition would sell any better.
Arden Press should reissue Lionel Fry's chemistry textbook despite Fry's objection, because every error found in the textbook can now be corrected in a new edition.
Lattice Press should not reissue Ana Voss's field guide, because Voss has died and much of the information in the guide has since become out of date.
questions.explanation: The principle states only necessary conditions for reissuing: consent and the ability to correct errors. It can therefore justify a decision not to reissue when one condition fails, as in (B), where the errors cannot be corrected. (A) is the trap: both conditions are met, but meeting necessary conditions does not show that a book should be reissued. (E) fails because Voss's estate might consent and outdated information might be correctable; (D) concludes the opposite of what the principle requires.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Reissue an out-of-print book → author (or estate) consents AND errors found since publication can be corrected. Contrapositive: no consent OR uncorrectable errors → don't reissue.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Look for a "should not reissue" verdict where one of the two conditions clearly fails.

breakdown.analysis: "Only if" means the principle lists requirements. It can tell you not to reissue when a requirement fails. It can never tell you to reissue. So the right answer must (1) conclude "should not reissue" and (2) show consent missing or errors uncorrectable. Lesson: meeting necessary conditions doesn't make something required.

choices.note: The trap. Both conditions are met, but necessary conditions can't justify "should reissue." They only open the door.
CORRECT. The estate consents, but the errors can't be corrected. The correction condition fails, so the principle says don't reissue. Both requirements of the application are met.
Poor sales aren't one of the principle's conditions. The principle can't justify this verdict.
Violates the consent requirement. Fry objects, so the principle says don't reissue. This concludes the opposite.
Tempting, since it's a "should not." But no condition is shown to fail: Voss's death doesn't rule out her estate's consent, and nothing says the outdated material couldn't be corrected.

questions.stimulus: Tech analyst: Brightway Software earned more profit last year than any other company in its industry, and its profit margin was the highest as well. Brightway's tablet division, although it brings in only a small share of the company's revenue, must therefore be more profitable than the tablet divisions of Brightway's competitors.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the tech analyst's reasoning?
choices: It relies on a comparison between Brightway and companies that may not operate in the same industry.
It confuses the amount of revenue that a company's division brings in with the amount of profit that it earns.
It takes for granted that a company's most profitable division must be the one that brings in most of its revenue.
It infers that a part of a company has a certain feature merely because the whole company has it.
It fails to consider that Brightway's competitors may become more profitable than Brightway in the coming years.
questions.explanation: Brightway's profitability as a whole is used to draw a conclusion about one division, though a highly profitable company can include an unprofitable division: (D). (B) is tempting because revenue is mentioned, but the argument never treats revenue as profit; it mentions revenue only to note that the division is small. (E) concerns the future, which the argument does not address.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Brightway's tablet division must be more profitable than its competitors' tablet divisions.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Brightway earned the most profit and had the highest margin in its industry; the tablet division brings in only a small share of revenue.

breakdown.analysis: Whole-to-part flaw. A company can top its industry because of one blockbuster division while another division loses money. It's like saying the richest family on the block must have the richest teenager on the block. Prephrase: it assumes what's true of the company is true of each division. This is the part/whole (division) flaw; worth knowing.

choices.note: The comparison is to Brightway's competitors in its own industry. No cross-industry comparison.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our bakery earns more than the city's biggest law firm, so we must be the best-run bakery in town.

choices.note: Tempting because revenue appears, but it's only there to note the division is small. The argument never treats revenue as profit.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our store had record sales this year, so it must have had record profits.

choices.note: The argument never says which division is most profitable or ties profit to revenue share.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The phone division is our most profitable, so it must account for most of our sales.

choices.note: CORRECT. The analyst moves from "the company is most profitable" to "this division beats rivals' divisions." A profitable company can have a weak division.
The argument is about last year, not the future. Off topic.
choices.example: Example of flaw: We lead the market today, so no competitor will ever catch up.

questions.stimulus: In the coastal city of Pellmouth, the number of summer days on which the temperature exceeds 35°C has risen steadily over the past thirty years. Over the same period, however, the number of people admitted to Pellmouth's hospitals each summer for heat-related illness has fallen, even though the city's population has grown slightly.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above EXCEPT:
choices: Most of the people admitted to Pellmouth's hospitals for heat-related illness are admitted on days when the temperature exceeds 35°C.
Over those thirty years, the share of Pellmouth homes with air conditioning has risen from under a fifth to nearly nine-tenths.
Fifteen years ago Pellmouth began opening air-conditioned public cooling centers on every day forecast to exceed 35°C.
Pellmouth's clinics now treat many cases of mild heat illness that formerly would have been sent to a hospital.
Over the past thirty years, a growing share of Pellmouth's elderly residents have moved to cooler inland towns.
questions.explanation: Four answers describe changes that would cut heat admissions even as heat rose: home air conditioning (B), cooling centers (C), clinics absorbing mild cases (D), and the departure of vulnerable residents (E). (A) explains nothing; if admissions cluster on very hot days, more very hot days should have raised admissions, so it deepens the puzzle. The trap in an EXCEPT question is to pick the first answer that doesn't sound like an explanation of heat itself, such as (D), which resolves the puzzle through how cases are counted.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Very hot days (over 35°C) in Pellmouth have steadily increased for thirty years, and the population grew a bit, but summer hospital admissions for heat illness have fallen.

breakdown.analysis: More heat, slightly more people, fewer heat admissions. Four answers will show some change over the thirty years that made people less likely to end up in the hospital for heat. We want the one that doesn't. Since this is a trend over time, a fixed fact that doesn't change over time can't explain it. Lesson: in EXCEPT questions, cross off the four that work and pick the leftover.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the exception. A fixed pattern, not a change. And if admissions happen mostly on very hot days, more very hot days should mean more admissions. It deepens the puzzle instead of resolving it.
Resolves it. Far more people can cool off at home, so fewer end up in the hospital despite more scorching days.
Resolves it. Public cooling centers on the hottest days protect people who'd otherwise get sick.
Resolves it, though sneakily. Heat illness might not have fallen, but hospital admissions would, because clinics now handle mild cases. The question asks about admissions.
Resolves it. The most heat-vulnerable group is shrinking in the city, so fewer admissions even with more heat.

questions.stimulus: Firefly species attract mates with species-specific patterns of flashes. Females of a few predatory firefly species, however, mimic the flash patterns of other species' females, luring males of those species and then eating them. The mimics tend to make small timing errors when they repeat a pattern, so males of prey species that respond only after watching a female's signal several times are eaten less often than males that respond at once. Thus, ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: the females of prey species repeat their signals several times in order to help males avoid being eaten
males of prey species cannot distinguish the signals of their own species' females from those of the mimics
the predatory mimics reproduce flash patterns more accurately than do the very females they are imitating
most males of prey species that live near the mimics are eaten before they ever have a chance to mate
where such mimics are common, prey males that respond slowly probably survive at higher rates
questions.explanation: Males that wait are eaten less often, and that difference matters most where mimics are common, so delaying males should survive at higher rates there: (E). (A) is attractive, but nothing indicates why females repeat their signals, let alone that they do so to protect males. (B) contradicts the claim that watching repetitions helps males avoid mimics, (C) contradicts the timing errors, and (D) is far stronger than the evidence.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Fireflies attract mates with species-specific flash patterns; 2. some predatory females mimic other species' patterns to lure and eat males; 3. mimics make small timing errors when repeating a pattern; 4. prey males that wait to watch a signal several times are eaten less often than males that respond at once.

breakdown.analysis: Waiting males get eaten less often. Where does that edge matter most? Where there are lots of mimics. So in mimic-heavy areas, waiting males probably survive at higher rates. Keep the completion modest and tied directly to the facts. Watch for answers that guess at purposes or invent numbers.

choices.note: Tempting, but it assigns a purpose. We're never told why females repeat signals, let alone that they do it to protect males.
Contradicts the facts. Waiting males do better because they can catch the mimics' timing errors, so they can tell the signals apart.
Contradicts the facts: the mimics make timing errors, so they're less accurate, not more.
"Most males are eaten" is far stronger than anything given. No numbers at all.
CORRECT. Waiting males are eaten less often, and that matters most where mimics are common, so delaying males probably survive at higher rates there. Hedged and directly supported.

questions.stimulus: Whenever a generic version of a drug becomes available, Ostrand Pharmacy stocks it, provided that Ostrand's suppliers can deliver it reliably. Those suppliers can reliably deliver any drug that is made in a facility that passed its most recent national inspection. A generic version of the asthma drug Brelomax has just become available. So Ostrand will stock generic Brelomax.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Ostrand's suppliers can reliably deliver only drugs made in facilities that passed their latest national inspections.
The brand-name version of Brelomax is made in a facility that passed its latest national inspection.
The facility in which the new generic Brelomax is made passed its most recent national inspection.
Ostrand stocks no generic drug that its suppliers are unable to deliver reliably.
Generic Brelomax is as effective in treating asthma as the brand-name version is.
questions.explanation: The chain is: made in an inspected facility, therefore reliably deliverable; available and reliably deliverable, therefore stocked. The only missing link is that generic Brelomax comes from an inspected facility, which (C) supplies. (A) and (D) reverse the conditionals, turning sufficient conditions into necessary ones, so neither establishes that the drug will be stocked. (B) concerns the wrong version of the drug.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ostrand will stock generic Brelomax.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Generic available AND suppliers can deliver reliably → stocked; made in a facility that passed its latest inspection → suppliers can deliver reliably; generic Brelomax just became available.

breakdown.analysis: We have "available." We still need "reliable delivery," and the only way in is the inspection rule. Chain: generic Brelomax's facility passed inspection → reliable delivery → (with available) → stocked. We need an answer that gets generic Brelomax into that first box.

choices.note: Reverses the inspection rule. "Only" makes inspection a requirement for reliable delivery, which still doesn't tell us generic Brelomax meets it.
Tempting because it uses the right words, but it's the wrong drug. Where the brand-name version is made tells us nothing about the generic.
CORRECT. Inspected facility → reliable delivery. Generic Brelomax is available and reliably deliverable → stocked. The chain is complete.
Reverses the stocking rule. It tells us what Ostrand won't stock, never that it will stock Brelomax.
Effectiveness isn't part of any rule. Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Media critic: Some newspapers now let readers vote online on which stories receive follow-up coverage. Supporters claim that this practice makes journalism more responsive to the public. In fact, it is likely to make journalism less responsive. The readers who bother to vote are mostly those already devoted to a few favorite topics, so the stories chosen will tend to reflect the interests of a small, unrepresentative group rather than those of the public at large.
questions.stem: The claim that the stories chosen will tend to reflect the interests of a small, unrepresentative group plays which one of the following roles in the media critic's argument?
choices: It is the main conclusion that the media critic's argument as a whole is intended to establish.
It is a conclusion supported by another claim in the argument and offered in support of the main conclusion.
It is a claim made by supporters of the practice that the media critic's argument attempts to refute.
It is a premise offered in support of the claim that the readers who vote are mostly devoted to a few topics.
It is a concession that the critic acknowledges but argues is irrelevant to the argument's main conclusion.
questions.explanation: The critic's main conclusion is that the practice is likely to make journalism less responsive. The claim in question follows from the premise about who votes (note the 'so') and in turn explains why responsiveness will decline, making it an intermediate conclusion: (B). (A) is the tempting trap because the claim is the last sentence, but it serves the claim that the practice will make journalism less responsive. (D) reverses the direction of support.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Letting readers vote on follow-up stories is likely to make journalism less responsive to the public.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Readers who vote are mostly devoted to a few favorite topics; so the stories chosen will reflect a small, unrepresentative group's interests rather than the public's.

breakdown.analysis: Three layers. 1. Bottom: who votes (devoted fans of a few topics). 2. Middle: "so" the chosen stories reflect a small, unrepresentative group. 3. Top: "In fact, it is likely to make journalism less responsive." The claim in question is the middle layer: supported by 1, supporting 3. Lesson: the last sentence isn't always the conclusion.

choices.note: Tempting, since it's the last sentence. But it explains why the practice will make journalism less responsive. That earlier claim is the main point.
CORRECT. It follows from the premise about who votes, signaled by "so," and it supports the main conclusion that the practice will make journalism less responsive. Intermediate conclusion.
Supporters say the practice makes journalism more responsive. This claim is the critic's own reasoning, not the supporters'.
Reversed. The voter claim supports this one ("so"), not the other way around.
Not a concession. The critic relies on it; it's central to the argument.

questions.stimulus: Pottery from the ancient settlement of Ombra bears a distinctive spiral motif that has been found at only one other site in the region, the coastal settlement of Dessin, two hundred kilometers away. The earliest spiral-decorated pottery at Dessin is about a century younger than the earliest at Ombra. So people from Ombra probably settled at Dessin.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions most helps in evaluating the argument?
choices: Did the people of Ombra decorate objects other than pottery, such as tools or textiles, with spirals?
How many pieces of pottery, decorated and undecorated, have been excavated at Ombra and at Dessin?
Was the spiral-decorated pottery at Dessin made from clay found near Dessin or near Ombra?
Did the people of Dessin continue to use the spiral motif for some time after Ombra was abandoned?
Was Ombra a larger settlement than Dessin at the time when each settlement's population was at its peak?
questions.explanation: The pottery could have reached Dessin through trade rather than through settlers from Ombra. If the Dessin pots were made of Ombra clay, trade becomes likely and the argument weakens; if they were made of local clay, someone at Dessin was making Ombra-style pots, which supports settlement. So (C) helps either way. (D) is tempting, but continued use of the motif at Dessin fits both settlement and later imitation, so neither answer settles much.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: People from Ombra probably settled at Dessin.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A distinctive spiral motif appears only at Ombra and Dessin (200 km apart); the earliest spiral pottery at Dessin is about a century younger than Ombra's.

breakdown.analysis: Shared pottery could mean settlers. Could it also mean trade, with Ombra pots shipped to Dessin? A good evaluate answer separates those two. Where was the Dessin pottery made? Ombra clay → probably shipped in, so trade, weakening the argument. Dessin clay → someone at Dessin was making Ombra-style pots, which fits settlers. Either answer moves the argument.

choices.note: Spirals on other objects at Ombra don't tell us how the motif got to Dessin.
Pottery counts tell us nothing about the link between the two sites.

CORRECT. Ombra clay → the pots were likely traded, not made by settlers, so the argument weakens. Dessin clay → people at Dessin knew Ombra's style firsthand, supporting settlement. Either answer matters.
Tempting, but continued use fits both settlers who stayed and locals who copied the style. Neither answer settles much.
A bigger Ombra might make migration slightly more plausible, but either answer leaves trade vs. settlement wide open.

questions.stimulus: Pharmacy analyst: Last year Medway Pharmacies began sending a text message to customers who had opted in to the service whenever one of their prescriptions was due for a refill. Among those customers, the proportion of refills picked up on time rose from 61 percent the year before to 78 percent. The messages, therefore, were responsible for the rise.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the analyst's argument?
choices: In a survey, most customers who received the messages described them as helpful and said that they hoped the service would continue indefinitely.
Nearly every customer who signed up for the service received at least one refill message last year, and most of them received several.
Last year several competing pharmacies in the area closed, and many of their former customers began filling prescriptions at Medway.
The text messages that Medway sent last year also announced discounts on nonprescription products sold in its stores.
Among Medway customers with no mobile number on file, who thus could not sign up, on-time refills were unchanged last year.
questions.explanation: The argument infers causation from a before-and-after change in one group, so it is open to the possibility that something pharmacy-wide, such as new pickup hours or an insurance rule, raised on-time refills for everyone. (E) supplies a control group: customers who could not receive the messages showed no rise, which points to the messages. (B) is the trap: it seems to confirm that the messages reached people, but the stimulus already says a message went out whenever a refill came due, so (B) adds nothing about what caused the rise. (A) offers only impressions; (C) and (D) do not separate the messages from other causes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Medway's refill text messages were responsible for the rise in on-time refills.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Among customers who signed up for the texts, on-time refills rose from 61 percent the year before to 78 percent.

breakdown.analysis: So the rate went up after the texts started. Did the texts do it, or did something else change at Medway that year for everybody? A before-and-after comparison in one group can't tell those apart. It's like: I started taking vitamins in May and felt better in June, so the vitamins worked. Maybe June was just sunnier. We need an answer that shows the rise didn't happen to comparable people who got no texts. Most students pick (B) because it sounds like proof the texts actually reached people. It fails because the stimulus already tells you a message went out whenever a refill came due. Confirming a fact the argument already gives you is irrelevant corroboration: it does nothing to rule out another cause. The right answer hides behind a stand-in description: customers with no mobile number on file are simply people who couldn't get the texts.

choices.note: Wrong. Customers liking the service doesn't show it changed their behavior. People can find a reminder helpful and still be late, or be on time for other reasons.

Tempting. It feels like it confirms exposure to the texts. But the premise already says a text went out whenever a refill was due, so this tells you nothing new. It doesn't touch the real question: was something else responsible for the rise?

Wrong. New customers from closed pharmacies are a different group from the customers whose rates were compared. If anything this muddies the comparison; it certainly doesn't support the texts as the cause.

Wrong. This tells you what else the texts said, not whether the texts caused the rise. It does nothing to rule out a pharmacy-wide change, and the discount angle could even suggest a different reason people came in.

CORRECT. These are the customers who couldn't get the texts: a control group. Their on-time rate stayed flat, so whatever raised the signed-up customers' rate wasn't something that hit all Medway customers. That makes the texts the likelier cause.

questions.stimulus: Any ancient structure aligned precisely with the sunrise on the summer solstice was built by people who tracked the sun's yearly movements over many years. People who tracked the sun's movements over that long a period must have kept some form of lasting record. The stone ring at Hallow Fen is aligned precisely with the summer solstice sunrise. Therefore, the builders of the Hallow Fen ring possessed a system of writing.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?
choices: Any people who possessed a system of writing kept lasting records of the sun's yearly movements.
Any people who kept a lasting record of any kind must have possessed a system of writing.
Most ancient structures aligned with the summer solstice sunrise were built by people with a system of writing.
The builders of the Hallow Fen ring tracked the sun's yearly movements over a period of many years.
Some ancient people who kept lasting records of the sun's movements possessed a system of writing.
questions.explanation: The premises establish that the ring's builders kept some form of lasting record; the conclusion requires that they had writing. (B) bridges that gap: anyone who kept any lasting record had writing. (A) reverses the needed conditional. (C) and (E) are tempting because they link alignment or record-keeping to writing, but 'most' and 'some' cannot guarantee that these particular builders had writing. (D) merely restates what the premises already establish.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The builders of the Hallow Fen ring possessed a system of writing.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Aligned with solstice sunrise → builders tracked the sun over many years; tracked that long → kept some lasting record; the Hallow Fen ring is aligned.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: aligned → long-term tracking → kept a lasting record. The conclusion jumps to "had writing," a brand-new term. Missing link: kept a lasting record → had writing. With it: aligned → tracked → record → writing. Notice how strong it has to be: a notched stick counts as a lasting record, so the bridge has to cover any record. In sufficient assumption, strong is fine.

choices.note: Reversed. Writing → records. We need records → writing.
CORRECT. Any lasting record → writing. The Hallow Fen builders kept a lasting record, so they had writing. The chain is complete.
Tempting, but "most" can't guarantee these builders had writing. Hallow Fen could be an exception.
Already established by the premises (aligned → tracked). Restating it doesn't bridge to writing.
"Some" record-keepers had writing says nothing certain about these particular builders.

questions.stimulus: Ten years ago, snowboarders accounted for 45 percent of the injured people treated at the first-aid clinic of the Haldane ski resort. Last season they accounted for only 30 percent. Over the same period, the resort required all of its snowboard instructors to complete a new safety course. Clearly, snowboarding at Haldane has become less dangerous than it was ten years ago.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: fails to consider that snowboarders may now make up a smaller share of the resort's visitors
takes for granted that the new safety course for snowboard instructors is responsible for the reduction in injuries
infers that snowboarding has become less dangerous at all ski resorts from evidence about only one resort
overlooks the possibility that skiing at Haldane has also become less dangerous over the past ten years
presumes, without providing justification, that a risk that has fallen over ten years will continue to fall in the future
questions.explanation: A falling share of the clinic's patients does not show that snowboarding became safer; if snowboarders became a smaller share of visitors, their share of injuries would fall even if each snowboarder's risk stayed the same or rose. (A) names that gap. (B) is the trap: the safety course is mentioned, but the argument never claims the course caused anything. (D) points the wrong way, and (C) and (E) describe conclusions the argument does not draw.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Snowboarding at Haldane has become less dangerous than it was ten years ago.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Snowboarders were 45% of the clinic's injured patients ten years ago and 30% last season; meanwhile, snowboard instructors took a new safety course.

breakdown.analysis: Snowboarders' share of the injuries fell. So what? A share depends on who else is on the mountain. If ten years ago half the visitors were snowboarders and now only a fifth are, then snowboarders making up 30% of injuries means they're getting hurt more per person, not less. We need an answer that says the mix of visitors may have changed. This is the percent-versus-rate confusion; know it.

choices.note: CORRECT. Danger is about the risk per snowboarder. If snowboarders became a smaller slice of the resort's visitors, their slice of the injuries could shrink even while each snowboarder's risk held steady or rose.
Tempting, because the course is sitting right there. But the conclusion is only that snowboarding got safer, not why. The argument never blames or credits the course.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Crime fell after the new mayor took office, so the new mayor's policies must have reduced crime.

choices.note: The conclusion is about Haldane only. No other resort is mentioned.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Injuries fell at our resort, so skiing has become safer everywhere.

choices.note: Wrong direction. Safer skiing would push the snowboarders' share of injuries up, not down. It's the opposite case, more skier injuries, that would explain the falling share.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Burglaries in our town fell after the new alarm law, so the law worked, overlooking that burglaries fell just as much in towns without the law.

choices.note: The argument makes no prediction. It's only about the change so far.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Accidents dropped for three years, so they will keep dropping next year.

questions.stimulus: Entomologist: Ant species on the island of Tavor differ widely in their habits. Every ant species there that cultivates fungus keeps the interior of its nests humid. Most of the island's ant species that keep their nests humid build those nests underground, and none of Tavor's ant species that nest underground forage at night. Several ant species on Tavor do forage at night.
questions.stem: If the entomologist's statements are true, which one of the following is most strongly supported by them?
choices: Fewer than half of Tavor's ant species with humid nests forage at night.
None of the ant species on Tavor that cultivate fungus inside their nests forage at night.
Most of the ant species on Tavor that cultivate fungus build their nests underground.
At least some of the ant species on Tavor that forage at night are species that cultivate fungus in their nests.
Several of the ant species on Tavor that cultivate fungus forage for food at night.
questions.explanation: Most humid-nest species nest underground, and no underground nester forages at night, so most humid-nest species do not forage at night; that means fewer than half of them do, which is (A) stated the other way around. (C) is the main trap: fungus cultivators are only a subset of the humid-nest species, and that subset could sit entirely in the minority that nests above ground. For the same reason (B), (D), and (E) are left open.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Fungus cultivator → humid nest; 2. Most humid-nest species → underground; 3. Underground → no night foraging; 4. Several species forage at night.

breakdown.analysis: Chain what actually links. Most humid-nest species are underground, and every underground species skips night foraging. Most + all chains: most humid-nest species don't forage at night. Now flip that into a count: if more than half don't, then fewer than half do. That's (A), dressed up so it doesn't look like the chain you just built. Most students pick (C) because fungus → humid → (most) underground looks like a clean chain. It fails because 'most humid-nest species' says nothing about which ones. The fungus cultivators are a subset of the humid-nest group, and 'most' isn't 'all': they could all be in the above-ground minority. Imagine 10 humid-nest species, 7 underground; the 3 above ground could be the only fungus cultivators.

choices.note: CORRECT. More than half of the humid-nest species are underground, and underground species never forage at night, so more than half of the humid-nest species don't forage at night. Fewer than half can be night foragers.
Wrong. Fungus cultivators might all be above-ground nesters, and nothing stops above-ground species from foraging at night. Too strong.
Tempting. It chains fungus → humid → underground. But the 'most' link covers humid-nest species in general, not the fungus-growing subset. That subset could be entirely in the above-ground minority.
Wrong. The night foragers could all be species with dry nests. Nothing ties night foraging to fungus.
Wrong. Possible, but nothing requires it. The several night foragers could be species that grow no fungus at all.

questions.stimulus: A therapist should not tell a client that a treatment will work when the evidence shows only that it often works. Overstating a treatment's prospects may persuade a client to begin it. But a client who later finds the promise broken will be less willing to trust the therapist at the times when that trust matters most.
questions.stem: The principle underlying the argument above is most similar to the principle underlying which one of the following arguments?
choices: A doctor should tell patients about every possible side effect of a medication, since patients who are caught off guard by a side effect may decide to stop taking the medication altogether.
A salesperson should not exaggerate a product's benefits in order to close a sale, because exaggerating is dishonest whether or not any customer is ever actually harmed by it in any way.
A teacher should praise students' efforts rather than their results, because students who are praised for their efforts tend to work harder and to persist longer on all of their later assignments.
A coach should not guarantee an athlete a team spot for following a plan: the promise may motivate now, but if broken, the athlete will heed the coach less when it counts.
A manager should not promise an employee a raise that she lacks the authority to grant, since her own supervisors may then penalize her for committing the company to something without permission.
questions.explanation: The principle: do not overstate the likely benefit of a course of action to get someone to adopt it, because the broken promise will erode trust you will need later. (D) matches every element: the overstatement, the short-term persuasion, and the later loss of trust. (B) is the trap: it condemns the same kind of exaggeration but justifies the condemnation by dishonesty alone, not by its effect on future trust. (E) rests on harm to the promiser rather than on lost trust.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: A therapist should not tell a client a treatment will work when evidence shows only that it often works.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Overstating may persuade the client to start, but when the promise breaks, the client will trust the therapist less when trust matters most.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Don't overstate X's prospects to get someone to act; the short-term persuasion is outweighed by the trust you'll lose and need later.

breakdown.analysis: The principle has a specific reason. Not "lying is wrong," but "the broken promise will cost you trust later, when you need it." The match needs all three pieces: 1. an overstated promise; 2. a short-term payoff; 3. damaged trust later. Lesson: in principle matching, the reason matters as much as the rule.

choices.note: About disclosing side effects, not overstating benefits. And the worry is patients quitting the drug, not losing trust in the doctor.
Tempting. Same "don't exaggerate," but the reason is dishonesty itself, regardless of consequences. The original's reason is the later loss of trust.
About what to praise, not about overstating anything. Different principle.
CORRECT. Overstated promise (a guaranteed spot), short-term gain (motivates now), later cost (the athlete heeds the coach less when it counts). Every element lines up.
The cost falls on the manager, penalized by her supervisors, not on the employee's trust. Different reason.

questions.stimulus: Ethicist: When the software firm Lumetra discovered a security flaw in its messaging app, it fixed the flaw within a week but chose not to tell users, on the grounds that there was no evidence the flaw had ever been exploited. Lumetra acted wrongly. People who sent sensitive messages during the months the flaw existed had a stake in knowing that those messages might have been exposed, even though they probably were not.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethicist's argument?
choices: A company should tell users about a security flaw in its product whenever there is any evidence that the flaw has actually been exploited.
A company should fix any security flaw in its products as soon as it reasonably can after the flaw has first been discovered.
A company that conceals a security flaw from its users acts wrongly only if the concealment results in some actual harm to them.
It is wrong to withhold information about a risk to people's interests from them, even if the risk was unlikely to materialize.
People who choose to send sensitive messages through an app thereby accept responsibility for whatever risks come with doing so.
questions.explanation: The ethicist rejects Lumetra's excuse that exploitation was unlikely and says users' stake in knowing settled the matter. (D) makes withholding information about a risk to people's interests wrong even when the risk was improbable, which is exactly Lumetra's case. (A) is the trap: it is pro-disclosure, but it applies only when there is evidence of exploitation, and here there was none. (B) is satisfied by Lumetra, and (C) and (E) cut against the ethicist.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Lumetra acted wrongly in not telling users about the flaw.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Users who sent sensitive messages had a stake in knowing those messages might have been exposed, even though they probably weren't.

breakdown.analysis: Lumetra's excuse: no evidence anyone exploited the flaw. The ethicist's answer: doesn't matter, users had a stake in knowing. So we need a principle that says the stake is what counts, and low probability is no excuse. A principle-justify answer has to tell you that what Lumetra did was wrong in these facts. Most students pick (A) because it is the pro-disclosure rule and the ethicist is pro-disclosure. It fails because its trigger is 'any evidence that the flaw has actually been exploited,' and the stimulus says there was none. A rule that doesn't apply to the facts can't justify a verdict on them. (D) hides behind synonyms: 'interests' for 'stake,' 'unlikely to materialize' for 'probably were not.'

choices.note: Tempting. It sounds like the ethicist's side. But it only kicks in when there is evidence of exploitation, and Lumetra had none. The ethicist's whole point is that disclosure was owed anyway.
Wrong. Lumetra fixed the flaw within a week, so this principle, if anything, says Lumetra did fine. The issue is telling users, not fixing.
Wrong. This undercuts the ethicist. The messages probably weren't exposed, so there was probably no actual harm, and by this rule Lumetra probably didn't act wrongly.

CORRECT. Lumetra withheld information about a risk to users' interests (possible exposure of sensitive messages), and the risk was unlikely to materialize. This principle says that's still wrong, which is exactly the ethicist's conclusion.
Wrong. This shifts responsibility to users, which cuts against the claim that Lumetra did wrong.

questions.stimulus: Most of the novels that Starling House published last year were written by first-time novelists. And according to an industry survey, most first-time novelists whose books were published last year received advances of less than $5,000. So most of the novels Starling House published last year earned their authors advances of less than $5,000.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: Most of the plants that the Hadley greenhouse sold last year were orchids. And according to a growers' survey, every orchid sold last year needed daily misting. So most of the plants Hadley sold last year needed daily misting.
Most members of the Orrin hiking club are retirees, and most of the club's own retirees go on a hike every week. So at least some members of the Orrin hiking club go on a hike every week.
Most residents of the town of Calder own bicycles, and most residents of Calder also own cars. So it must be that at least some of the residents of Calder own both a bicycle and a car.
Most applicants to the Velor fellowship are from the town of Varn, and most of the fellowship's recipients are from Varn as well. So most applicants from Varn end up receiving the fellowship.

Most electric cars sold in the region last month cost over $40,000, and most of the cars that Dunmore Motors sold last month were electric. So most of the cars that Dunmore sold last month cost over $40,000.
questions.explanation: The argument applies a majority figure about first-time novelists in general to Starling's first-time novelists, who could be the minority with large advances; and even a representative 'most of most' need not be a majority. (E) makes the same move with its premises swapped: Dunmore's electric cars might be the cheaper minority. (A) is the trap: it copies the stimulus almost word for word, but its second premise says 'every,' which makes the conclusion valid. (B) and (C) are valid, and (D) commits a different error.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most novels Starling House published last year earned advances under $5,000.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most Starling novels last year were by first-time novelists; most first-time novelists published last year (industry-wide) got advances under $5,000.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most of group X are B; most B in general are C; so most of X are C.

breakdown.analysis: Who says Starling's first-timers look like first-timers in general? Starling could be the press that pays its debut authors well. And even if they were typical, most of most can be a minority: 60 percent of 60 percent is 36 percent. Find the answer that applies a general 'most' to one seller's or publisher's subgroup. Most students pick (A) because it looks like a copy: same 'Most of the … last year were …', same 'according to a survey', same conclusion. It fails because its second premise says 'every' orchid, and most + all is valid. A valid version of a flawed argument is never the parallel flaw. (E) is easy to skip because it puts the general premise first, but the skeleton is identical.

choices.note: Tempting. It mirrors the stimulus sentence by sentence. But 'every orchid sold last year needed misting' covers Hadley's orchids too, so most of Hadley's plants needed misting. Valid, so not the same flaw.
Wrong. The second premise is about the club's own retirees, and the conclusion is only 'at least some'. Most of a majority is at least one member. Valid.
Wrong. Two majorities of the same town must overlap, so at least some residents own both. Valid.
Wrong. Flawed, but differently: it confuses where recipients come from with the chance that a Varn applicant wins. That's a reversal of 'most', not a general-to-subgroup move.

CORRECT. A general fact about electric cars in the region is applied to Dunmore's electric cars, which could be the cheap minority, and two 'mosts' are chained. Same flaw, premises in the other order.

questions.stimulus: Apartment rents in downtown Ferrisport have risen 30 percent in just three years, and the share of downtown apartments standing vacant is the lowest in decades. Meanwhile, many downtown office buildings stand largely empty, and their owners are eager to sell. So a developer who bought these office buildings and converted them into apartments would find the investment highly profitable.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Apartment rents in Ferrisport's suburbs have risen far less over the past three years than rents downtown have.
The downtown units whose rents have climbed nearly all have windows in every room, which the offices' deep floor plans cannot provide.
Developers in Ferrisport have generally earned higher returns from building new apartment complexes than from converting existing buildings.
Over the past decade, Ferrisport's downtown population has grown considerably faster than the city's supply of downtown housing has.
Many of the office tenants who have left downtown Ferrisport moved to newer and cheaper office space in the suburbs.
questions.explanation: The argument assumes that converted offices would earn the rents downtown apartments now command. (B) shows the rent surge is for a kind of unit the office buildings cannot become, so converted units may not share in it. (C) is the trap: it says conversion earns less than new construction, but a comparison with another investment does not show that conversion would not be highly profitable. (D) strengthens, and (A) and (E) do not bear on converted units' rents.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Converting the empty downtown office buildings into apartments would be highly profitable.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Downtown rents are up 30 percent in three years and vacancy is at a decades low; many office buildings are empty and for sale.

breakdown.analysis: The argument treats 'downtown apartments' as one market. Would the converted units actually get those rents? Only if they're the kind of apartment renters are paying up for. It's like seeing that three-bedroom houses are selling fast and concluding your studio will too. We need an answer that shows converted offices wouldn't share in the rent boom. Most students pick (C) because 'lower returns' sounds like 'not profitable.' It fails because it's a comparison: conversion can earn less than new construction and still be highly profitable. Watch the switch from a relative claim (less profitable than) to an absolute one (highly profitable). (B) looks like a detail about windows until you see it splits the market.

choices.note: Wrong. Suburban rents aren't the issue. The conversions would be downtown, where rents are high.
CORRECT. The rent boom is in units with windows in every room. Deep office floor plans can't give that, so converted units would be outside the hot segment and may not command the high rents.

Tempting. It sounds like conversion is a worse deal. But 'less profitable than new construction' doesn't mean 'not highly profitable.' Both could be lucrative. A relative claim can't sink an absolute one.
Wrong. This strengthens the case: demand outpacing supply supports high rents for new units.
Wrong. This explains why the offices are empty. It says nothing about what converted apartments would earn.

questions.stimulus: Climatologist: Of the severe storms that struck the Lundar coast over the past decade, 70 percent were preceded by a week of unusually warm temperatures in the adjacent sea. Records of sea temperatures and storms for that decade are complete and reliable. Hence, whenever the sea off the Lundar coast has a week of unusually warm temperatures, a severe storm will probably follow.
questions.stem: The climatologist's argument is flawed because it
choices: treats a correlation between two kinds of events as proof that one causes the other
draws a general conclusion from data that cover too short a period to reveal any reliable long-term pattern
fails to consider that some of the severe storms struck the coast after weeks of entirely normal sea temperatures
presumes, without providing justification, that unusually warm seas are the only factor that can produce a severe storm
overlooks the possibility that most of the decade's unusually warm weeks were followed by no severe storm
questions.explanation: That most storms were preceded by warm weeks does not show that most warm weeks were followed by storms; warm weeks could be common and storms rare. (E) names exactly that overlooked possibility. (A) is the trap: correlation-to-causation is the textbook flaw, but the conclusion is a prediction ('will probably follow'), not a causal claim. (C) restates the 30 percent the premise already concedes, and a decade of reliable records, as in (B), is not the problem.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Whenever the sea has an unusually warm week, a severe storm will probably follow.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 70 percent of the decade's severe storms came after an unusually warm week; the records are complete and reliable.

breakdown.analysis: The premise starts from storms and looks back: most storms had a warm week first. The conclusion starts from warm weeks and looks forward: most warm weeks bring a storm. Those are different fractions. Quick numbers: 10 storms, 7 after warm weeks, but 50 warm weeks in the decade. Then only 7 of 50 warm weeks were followed by a storm. It's like: most lottery winners bought a ticket that week, so if you buy a ticket you'll probably win. Most students pick (A) because 'correlation is not causation' is the flaw everyone knows. It fails because the climatologist never claims warm seas cause storms; the conclusion is a probability claim. (E) hides in omission form: it's the reversed proportion stated as the case the argument ignores.

choices.note: Tempting. It's the classic flaw. But the conclusion never says warm water causes storms; it says a storm will probably follow. The error is in the proportions, not in a causal leap.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Cities with more libraries have lower crime, so building libraries causes crime to fall.

choices.note: Wrong. Ten years of complete, reliable records is a reasonable basis, and nothing suggests the period is too short. The problem would remain with a century of data.
choices.example: Example of flaw: It rained on both days I visited, so it rains there all the time.

choices.note: Wrong. The premise already concedes this: 30 percent of storms weren't preceded by warm weeks. The argument doesn't ignore it.
Wrong. The argument doesn't claim warm seas are the only cause. It openly allows that 30 percent of storms came without them.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Smoking causes lung disease, so anyone with lung disease must have smoked.

choices.note: CORRECT. If warm weeks were common, most of them could have passed with no storm at all, even though most storms followed a warm week. Then 'a storm will probably follow' is false.

questions.stimulus: Over the past five years, the Corvell Courier has lost half of its readers under the age of thirty. During the same period, young people have increasingly gotten their news from short online videos rather than from newspapers. So if the Courier begins producing short news videos of its own, it will win back many of the young readers it has lost.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: Producing short news videos is the only way for the Courier to win back any of its lost young readers.
Most young people prefer short online videos to every other source of news, including printed newspapers.
The young readers the Courier lost stopped reading it because they began getting their news from short videos.
Some of the young readers the Courier has lost would watch short news videos that the Courier produced.
Producing short news videos will not cost the Courier more than it can afford to spend on new projects.
questions.explanation: The argument predicts that the Courier's videos will win back lost young readers, which cannot happen unless some of those particular readers would watch the Courier's videos. Negate (D) and the prediction collapses. (C) is the attractive trap: those readers might have left for other reasons and still watch the Courier's videos, so the argument does not need it. (E) concerns whether the plan is affordable, not the prediction actually made, and (A) and (B) are far stronger than required.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: If the Courier produces short news videos, it will win back many of the young readers it lost.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The Courier lost half its under-30 readers in five years; young people increasingly get news from short online videos.

breakdown.analysis: The prediction is specific: these lost readers will come back through the Courier's videos. What's the minimum that has to be true? At least some of those lost readers would actually watch the Courier's videos. If none would, the plan can't win anyone back. Why they left doesn't strictly matter. Negation test.

choices.note: Too strong. Videos don't have to be the only way. Negated (other ways exist too), videos could still win readers back.
choices.negation: Producing short news videos is not the only way for the Courier to win back young readers.

choices.note: Too strong. Young people don't need to prefer videos to everything. Negated, enough of them could still watch the Courier's videos.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most young people prefer short online videos to every other source of news.

choices.note: Tempting, because it ties the two premises together. But those readers might have left for another reason, like a price increase, and still watch the Courier's videos. Negated, the plan can still work.
choices.negation: The young readers the Courier lost did not stop reading it because they began getting their news from short videos.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negated, none of the lost readers would watch the Courier's videos. Then the videos can't win any of them back, and the prediction collapses. Required.
choices.negation: None of the young readers the Courier has lost would watch short news videos produced by the Courier.

choices.note: About whether the plan is affordable, not whether it would win readers back. The prediction survives the negation.
choices.negation: Producing short news videos will cost the Courier more than it can afford.

passages.title: Solvang and the Honest Seam
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
In The Honest Seam (1987), the architectural critic Henrik Solvang argued that new work on a damaged historic building should be plainly distinguishable from the old in material, tooling, or color, so that a visitor can “read the building’s wounds.” Imitative repair, which reproduces lost parts in their original manner, Solvang regarded as a quiet forgery: it presents as the testimony of one age what is in fact the product of another. His model was the chapel at Strandholm, gutted by fire in 1944 and rebuilt in the 1950s with limestone of a slightly cooler gray and vault ribs left deliberately unmolded. The view soon became orthodoxy among conservation architects.

What Solvang fails to clarify is what “the old” is from which new work must be distinguished. Few buildings reach us in a single state. The Strandholm chapel itself had received a new west front in the 1720s and a new roof in the 1860s, yet the 1950s repairs were set off against all earlier fabric alike, as though the 1720s front were as original as the medieval nave. The seam Solvang praises is thus one cut among many, singled out chiefly because it is the most recent. His doctrine, in effect, requires only the latest intervention to announce itself.

The doctrine also rests on two undefended assumptions. It assumes that the principal relationship between a building and its public is evidentiary: the building is a document, and its public consists of visitors who come to read it. And it assumes that a distinction, once made, will remain visible.
