At Strandholm, the second assumption has not held: the cooler limestone has weathered within forty years to a near match with the surrounding stone, and the seam meant to testify now needs a guide to point it out.

Other complications run deeper. Some building traditions treat faithful reproduction as continuity rather than deceit. The Ise Grand Shrine in Japan has for centuries been rebuilt in the same form at intervals of roughly twenty years; to insist that each rebuilding look different would mistake what is being preserved: a practice of making rather than a particular set of timbers. The stave barns of the Ulvebrekk valley are repaired board by board by farmers for whom a barn is a tool to be kept in working order rather than a record to be consulted. And a conspicuous seam can mislead in its own way, suggesting a catastrophe where there was only routine maintenance. None of this shows that imitative repair is always right. Solvang was correct that a repair makes a claim about the past, and that such claims can be false. But whether a repair deceives depends on what the building is understood to be—document, instrument, or continuing practice—and that question must be answered before the question of seams can be.

passages.title: Participatory Budgeting
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Participatory budgeting—the practice of letting residents vote directly on how a portion of a city’s capital budget will be spent—has spread widely since its origins in Brazil in the late 1980s, and its advocates describe it as a remedy for civic disengagement. Its critics raise three objections. First, those who take part are not a fair sample of the city: the proposal meetings at which residents decide which projects will appear on the ballot are typically held on weeknight evenings, and they reward residents who have flexible schedules, reliable child care, and the confidence to speak in public. Second, the process is biased toward the visible. Residents predictably favor new playgrounds, murals, and bike lanes—things they can point to—over replacing aging water mains, so that a city allocating money this way may find its least glamorous infrastructure starved. Third, the process blurs accountability: when a poorly chosen project fails, council members can say that residents chose it, and residents chose it as a crowd.

The record of the program in Brennick, which in 2014 set aside 2 percent of its capital budget for residents to allocate directly, bears on the first two objections. Skeptics there predicted that the process would be captured by the handful of activists who dominate every public hearing. Yet because Brennick accepted ballots by mail and at libraries and grocery stores over a two-week period, the share of votes cast by residents of its lowest-income neighborhoods has exceeded those neighborhoods’ share of the city’s population in each of the program’s first eight cycles. Nor has the program crowded out ordinary obligations. Residents decide only how the set-aside is spent; the remaining 98 percent of the capital budget, including every dollar for water and sewer systems, is still allocated by the council. And the projects residents have chosen have often addressed problems that city engineers had overlooked—a dangerous pedestrian crossing near a senior center, for example, that had never appeared in a traffic study because no one had yet been killed there.

Brennick’s experience does not answer every objection; nothing in its design makes it easier to hold anyone to account for a failed project. But it suggests that the first two objections describe avoidable features of particular programs rather than flaws inherent in the practice. It also points to a benefit the critics overlook. Residents who have spent weeks weighing the cost of a new streetlight against that of a repaired sidewalk come away with a far clearer sense of the trade-offs every budget involves. Officials who dismiss such programs as symbolic because they control only a sliver of the budget are thus measuring them by the wrong yardstick: the size of the sums at stake rather than what residents learn in deciding how to spend them.

passages.title: Calder’s Rolling Beach Easement
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
Along the coast of the province of Calder, the public has long held a customary right to use the dry-sand beach, the strip between the high-water line and the line of permanent vegetation, even where it lies on privately titled land. The right was clear so long as the coast stayed put. But Calder’s shore moves. When erosion pushes the vegetation line inland, does the public’s easement move with it onto what was formerly a lawn or house lot, or stay fixed and vanish into the sea?

The Calder High Court answered in Ostrander v. Coastal Lands Board (1979). Borrowing from the older law of river boundaries, the court distinguished erosion, a gradual and imperceptible loss of land, from avulsion, a sudden and perceptible loss such as that caused by a single storm. The easement follows gradual change, so a beach that creeps inland carries the public’s right with it. But when a storm abruptly strips away the dunes, the easement stays put, and the exposed sand remains private unless natural processes rebuild the beach to its former position. Thus an owner whose dune line retreated thirty meters in one hurricane could fence the exposed sand, whereas a neighbor who lost the same thirty meters over twenty years could not.

Ostrander drew criticism from several directions. Landowners argued that a rolling easement shifted public use onto land they had never surrendered. Public access advocates raised a more practical objection: if most land loss on Calder’s coast occurs in storms, the avulsion exception would swallow the rule, and within a generation fences would line the shore. Coastal geologists doubted that the distinction could be applied at all, since much apparently gradual retreat is the cumulative work of many small storms, while a single storm’s losses are often partly reversed as sand returns in the following months. Judge Imelda Corran, dissenting, wrote that the majority had “imported a distinction made for rivers that move their channels to a shore that moves its sand.”

Later developments lent support to these critics. A provincial survey in 1996 found that in counties with frequent storms, owners had fenced more than a third of the formerly public dry beach, and that much of the fenced sand had partly rebuilt on its own. In Reyes v. Port Allard (2011), the court abandoned the speed-based test. It now asks only whether a shift in the vegetation line has persisted for five years: if it has, the easement moves to the new line however the shift occurred; if the line returns seaward within that period, nothing changes. Reyes has critics of its own, who call the five-year period arbitrary. But it has an evidentiary virtue that Ostrander lacked: it asks courts to determine where a line has stood, not to reconstruct how quickly it got there.

passages.title: Dark Eggs of the Kessin Sandpiper
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
For shorebirds that nest on open ground, egg color is usually the best defense: it closely matches the sand or pebbles of the nesting site, and experiments with artificial eggs confirm that well-matched eggs are found by predators far less often than mismatched ones. The Kessin sandpiper is a striking exception. Its breeding range runs some 2,000 kilometers from temperate coastal marshes to subarctic gravel plains, and its eggs grow steadily darker toward the north—even though the pale gravel of the northern sites makes dark eggs especially easy to spot.

The ornithologist Teodora Valk has proposed that the eggs’ darkness is an adaptation not for concealment but for warmth. Only the female Kessin sandpiper incubates, and because her mate does not feed her, she must leave the nest repeatedly each day to forage. While she is away, the eggs cool, and an embryo whose temperature falls below about 26°C stops developing until it is warmed again. Every such pause lengthens the incubation period, and every extra day in the nest is one more day on which a predator or storm can destroy the eggs. Dark shells absorb more sunlight than pale ones and so slow the eggs’ cooling. Where breeding-season air is cold, Valk contends, this benefit is large enough that the darkness pays for itself.

The arithmetic is clearest at a northern colony Valk studied, where air temperatures during incubation averaged 8°C and females’ foraging trips averaged about 25 minutes. Exposed to sunlight, a pale egg there cooled from its incubation temperature of 36°C to the 26°C threshold in about 15 minutes, so on a typical trip its embryo spent roughly 10 minutes with development halted. Over the 60 or so trips of a full incubation, those pauses added up to about 10 hours. A dark egg under the same conditions took about 28 minutes to reach the threshold—long enough, on most trips, to avoid any pause at all. At the southern end of the range, by contrast, where air temperatures averaged near 20°C, even pale eggs took more than an hour to cool to 26°C; there, darkening would buy no developmental time.

Two further observations support Valk’s account. First, egg darkness tracks breeding-season temperature more closely than it tracks latitude: of two colonies lying at the same latitude, one on a cold, wind-scoured island and the other in a sheltered inland valley, the island colony lays markedly darker eggs. Second, in northern colonies, nests with darker clutches hatched more often overall than nests with paler ones, even though, day for day, darker clutches were found by predators somewhat more often. The account leaves questions open—it does not explain why some northern females lay paler clutches than their neighbors—but it turns what looked like a lapse in camouflage into the predictable result of a trade-off between two dangers.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Solvang’s doctrine should give way to a general policy of imitative repair, which better respects the traditions within which many buildings were made.
Because new materials eventually weather to match old ones, distinguishable repair cannot be sustained over time, and Solvang’s doctrine therefore defeats its own purpose.
Whether a repair deceives depends on what a building is understood to be, a prior question that Solvang’s doctrine simply answers without argument.
Since few historic buildings reach us in a single state, conservation architects should abandon the very notion of a building’s original fabric.
Solvang rightly holds that repairs make claims about the past, but the rebuilding of the Strandholm chapel misapplied his own doctrine.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph states the thesis: whether a repair deceives depends on what the building is understood to be, and the third paragraph shows that Solvang simply assumes the answer (the building is a document). That is C. B inflates one complication, the weathering at Strandholm, into the thesis; A and D recommend policies the author never endorses (the author says imitative repair is not always right); E treats Strandholm as a misapplication, when the author uses it as the doctrine’s own model.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Main point: what is the author’s overall claim about Solvang’s doctrine?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Whole passage; the thesis is in the last three sentences of the fourth paragraph, and the 'undefended assumptions' in the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: So is the author attacking Solvang or not? Partly. Paragraph 1 lays out the doctrine, paragraphs 2–3 poke holes in it, and the fourth paragraph adds harder cases and then lands the conclusion: Solvang was right that repairs make claims about the past, but whether a repair deceives depends on what the building is understood to be, and that question comes first. Prephrase: 'Solvang's seam rule skips a prior question (what is the building?) that decides whether a repair deceives.' Watch for answers that turn a measured critique into a call to abandon the doctrine.

choices.note: Too strong. The author says outright that 'None of this shows that imitative repair is always right.' No general policy of imitation is recommended.
Tempting, because the weathering at Strandholm is real (third paragraph). But it's one complication among several, and the author never says the doctrine defeats itself.

CORRECT. The fourth paragraph says deception depends on what the building is understood to be, and the third paragraph says Solvang's doctrine just assumes the building is a document. 'Answers without argument' is the passage's 'undefended assumption' in synonyms.
Too strong. The author notes that buildings have many layers (second paragraph) but never says to drop the idea of original fabric.
Gets the concession right but misplaces the criticism. Strandholm is Solvang's model case, not a misapplication; the author's target is the doctrine itself.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Solvang’s attitude toward imitative repair can most accurately be described as one of
choices: ambivalence
disapproval
indifference
resignation
curiosity
questions.explanation: In the first paragraph Solvang calls imitative repair 'a quiet forgery' that presents the work of one age as the testimony of another, a plain stance of disapproval (B). Nothing suggests he is torn about it (A) or accepts it as unavoidable (D); his whole doctrine exists to rule it out.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Attitude of a cited figure (Solvang, not the author) toward imitative repair.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph, second sentence: Solvang 'regarded [it] as a quiet forgery.'

breakdown.analysis: Whose attitude? Solvang's, not the author's. Don't let the author's more sympathetic remarks about reproduction (fourth paragraph) leak in. Solvang calls imitative repair a forgery. Prephrase: he disapproves.

choices.note: Ambivalence means mixed feelings. Solvang has none here: 'forgery' is a one-sided word.
CORRECT. Calling a practice 'a quiet forgery' is disapproval, and his doctrine is built to exclude it.
Indifference is the opposite of what the passage shows. He cared enough to write a book against it.
Resignation would mean accepting it as unavoidable. He wants it replaced with distinguishable repair.
Curiosity has no support. He has already judged the practice.

questions.stem: The primary function of the third paragraph is to
choices: recount the history of alterations to the building that the critic used as his principal example of sound repair
present evidence that the critic’s recommended technique was carelessly executed at the building he most admired
introduce the alternative building traditions that are discussed in greater detail in the paragraph that follows
argue that most visitors to historic buildings take little interest in the evidence that repairs provide about the past
identify assumptions underlying the critic’s view and show that one of them fails in his own model case
questions.explanation: The third paragraph names two 'undefended assumptions' (that a building is a document and that a distinction stays visible) and shows the second failing at Strandholm, Solvang’s model. That is E. A describes the second paragraph; B misreads the fading seam, which is caused by forty years of weathering, not careless work; C and D describe things the paragraph does not do.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Paragraph function: what job does the third paragraph do in the argument?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph (begins 'The doctrine also rests on two undefended assumptions').

breakdown.analysis: Read the first sentence: 'The doctrine also rests on two undefended assumptions.' Then the paragraph names them (building as document; distinctions stay visible) and shows the second one breaking down at Strandholm. Prephrase: 'name the doctrine's hidden assumptions and show one failing in Solvang's own example.'

choices.note: That's the second paragraph (the 1720s front and 1860s roof). Right passage, wrong paragraph.
Tempting, because the seam did fail at Strandholm. But it failed because the stone weathered over forty years, not because the work was careless.
The traditions (Ise, the Ulvebrekk barns) first appear in the fourth paragraph; the third paragraph doesn't introduce them.
Too strong and off target. The paragraph identifies the 'evidentiary' assumption; it never argues that visitors don't care.
CORRECT. Two assumptions are identified, and the second ('a distinction, once made, will remain visible') is shown not to hold at Strandholm, his model case.

questions.stem: The passage raises all of the following as complications for Solvang’s doctrine EXCEPT:
choices: the expense of obtaining replacement materials that differ visibly from a building’s existing fabric
the tendency of contrasting new material to come to resemble the surrounding material over time
the existence of traditions in which faithful reproduction is understood as a form of continuity
the possibility that a conspicuous seam will lead viewers to infer an event that never occurred
the presence in many buildings of alterations made in several different periods
questions.explanation: Cost is never mentioned, so A is the exception. B is the weathering of the Strandholm limestone (third paragraph); C is the Ise Grand Shrine and the Ulvebrekk barns and D is the seam that suggests a catastrophe (both fourth paragraph); E is the point about the 1720s front and 1860s roof (second paragraph).

setup.label: Task
setup.text: EXCEPT question: four choices are complications the passage raises; find the one it doesn't.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second, third, and fourth paragraphs; check each choice against them.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, so tick off the four that appear. Layers of alterations: second paragraph. Weathering: third paragraph. Traditions of reproduction and a misleading seam: fourth paragraph. Whatever's left over is the answer. A choice that sounds like a sensible objection but never appears is the classic EXCEPT answer.

choices.note: CORRECT. Nothing in the passage mentions cost. It's a reasonable real-world worry, which is exactly why it's here.
Raised: the cooler limestone 'has weathered within forty years to a near match' (third paragraph).
Raised: Ise is rebuilt in the same form as continuity, and the barns are kept as tools (fourth paragraph).
Raised: a conspicuous seam can suggest 'a catastrophe where there was only routine maintenance' (fourth paragraph).
Raised: the chapel had a new west front in the 1720s and a new roof in the 1860s (second paragraph).

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Solvang’s position commits him to which one of the following views?
choices: The 1720s west front of the Strandholm chapel should be treated as new work rather than as part of the original fabric.
Imitative repair is acceptable when a building’s earlier alterations were themselves carried out in an imitative manner.
Buildings rebuilt at regular intervals in the same form are exempt from the requirement that repairs be distinguishable.
Any later repair to the portions of the Strandholm chapel rebuilt after the 1944 fire should be distinguishable from those portions.
The work done on the Strandholm chapel in the 1860s has less historical value than the work done there in the 1950s.
questions.explanation: Solvang’s rule is that new work must be plainly distinguishable from the old fabric it repairs, and the second paragraph says the doctrine in effect requires the latest intervention to announce itself. Once the post-fire rebuilding of the 1950s is itself existing fabric, a later repair to it must be set off from it too, which is D. A is the dominant trap: it sounds like the author’s criticism turned into a rule, but Solvang in effect treated the 1720s front as original, and the author only notes this without saying what should be done. C is the author’s complication, not Solvang’s view, and E confuses which work announces itself with which work is more valuable.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply Solvang's own rule to a new case and say what it forces him to accept.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1 (the rule: new work 'plainly distinguishable from the old'; Strandholm rebuilt in the 1950s after the 1944 fire); paragraph 2, last sentence ('requires only the latest intervention to announce itself').

breakdown.analysis: Solvang's rule: whatever is new must be visibly different from whatever is already there. So what happens when the 1950s repair is the thing being repaired? It's now 'the old', and the new patch must be distinguishable from it. The right answer refers to the 1950s work by a stand-in ('the portions rebuilt after the 1944 fire'), so you have to connect it back to paragraph 1. Most students pick (A) because the author's critique is all about the 1720s front, and (A) sounds like the fix. But the author describes what Solvang's approach did with the 1720s front ('as though ... as original as the medieval nave'). Solvang is committed to the opposite of (A), and the author never prescribes it either.

choices.note: Tempting. This is the trap. It turns the author's complaint into a rule. But Solvang's approach set the 1950s work off against 'all earlier fabric alike', treating the 1720s front as old. He's committed to the reverse, and the author doesn't recommend (A) either.
Solvang calls imitative repair 'a quiet forgery'. Nothing in his position creates this exception.
That's the author's Ise Grand Shrine complication. Solvang's doctrine has no such exemption; the whole point is that it ignores such traditions.

CORRECT. The fire-damaged portions were rebuilt in the 1950s. Under Solvang's rule, a later repair to them is new work, and new work must be distinguishable from the existing fabric, which now includes the 1950s work.
Value isn't the issue. The doctrine concerns which work must be visibly distinguished, not which work matters more historically.

questions.stem: With which one of the following statements would the author be most likely to agree?
choices: A repair plainly distinguishable from the surrounding fabric can still give a misleading impression of a building’s history.
A repair that follows a local tradition of faithful reproduction cannot misrepresent the history of the building it restores.
Conservation architects ought to abandon Solvang’s doctrine entirely in favor of judging each repair case by case.
How a building ought to be repaired is a more fundamental question than what that building is understood to be.
Visitors to the Strandholm chapel today can read its history more easily than visitors could when the repairs were new.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says a conspicuous seam 'can mislead in its own way,' suggesting a catastrophe where there was only routine maintenance, so a distinguishable repair can mislead. That is A. B goes too far: the author says only that some traditions treat reproduction as continuity, and adds that imitative repair is not always right. D reverses the author’s order of questions, and E reverses the weathering point, since the seam now needs a guide.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Author agreement: which statement fits the author's stated views?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, especially the sentence about a conspicuous seam misleading in its own way; also the third paragraph (weathering) for E.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, so test each choice against a specific sentence. The author's sharpest jab at Solvang is that his own preferred kind of repair, the visible seam, can also mislead: it can make a viewer infer a catastrophe that never happened. Look for that.

choices.note: CORRECT. Fourth paragraph: 'a conspicuous seam can mislead in its own way, suggesting a catastrophe where there was only routine maintenance.' A visible repair, misleading impression.
Too strong. The author says some traditions treat reproduction as continuity, then adds that imitative repair isn't always right. 'Cannot misrepresent' is far beyond that.
Too strong. The author says Solvang was correct about something and never calls for abandoning the doctrine.
Reversed. The author says the question of what the building is 'must be answered before the question of seams can be.'
Reversed. The seam has weathered to a near match and 'now needs a guide to point it out.' It's harder to read now, not easier.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Participatory budgeting has failed to remedy civic disengagement, because those who take part are not a fair sample of the cities that adopt it.
Brennick’s experience suggests that some objections to participatory budgeting describe avoidable flaws, and that the practice has a benefit its critics overlook.
Brennick’s program has answered every major objection raised by critics of participatory budgeting and should be adopted by other cities without modification.
Because participatory budgeting controls only a small share of a city’s capital budget, its effects on city finances are largely symbolic.
Participatory budgeting is valuable chiefly because residents tend to choose projects that address problems professional engineers have overlooked.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph draws the conclusion: Brennick’s record suggests the first two objections describe avoidable features of particular programs, and it points to a benefit (what residents learn) that critics overlook. That is B. A states the critics’ first objection as fact; C ignores the author’s concession that Brennick does not answer every objection; D is the officials’ view the author rejects; E inflates one supporting example into the main point.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Main point: what is the author's overall conclusion about participatory budgeting?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph (the conclusion), read against the objections in the first paragraph and the Brennick evidence in the second.

breakdown.analysis: Does the author side with the critics or the advocates? Mostly the advocates, with a concession. Paragraph 1 gives three objections; paragraph 2 gives Brennick's record against the first two; paragraph 3 concedes the third objection is unanswered, says the first two describe avoidable features, and adds a benefit: residents learn about trade-offs. Prephrase: 'Brennick shows some objections are avoidable, and the practice has an overlooked educational benefit.'

choices.note: That's the critics' first objection, and the author argues Brennick's design avoided it. Wrong party's view.
CORRECT. Matches the third paragraph: the first two objections describe 'avoidable features of particular programs,' and the program 'points to a benefit the critics overlook.'
Too strong. The author concedes Brennick 'does not answer every objection' (accountability), and nothing is said about adoption elsewhere.
Opposite. This is the dismissive officials' view, which the author says uses 'the wrong yardstick.'
Tempting, because the crossing example is vivid. But it's one supporting detail in the second paragraph; the author calls what residents learn the overlooked benefit.

questions.stem: According to the passage, critics contend that residents choosing among proposed projects tend to favor projects that
choices: cost the least to build and maintain over time
benefit the neighborhoods in which the residents live
have already been endorsed by the city’s council members
produce results that residents can readily see
repair or replace the city’s existing infrastructure, such as water mains
questions.explanation: The critics’ second objection is that residents 'predictably favor' playgrounds, murals, and bike lanes, 'things they can point to,' which is D. E reverses the point, since repairs like replacing water mains are what lose out. B may sound realistic, but the passage never says residents favor their own neighborhoods, and A and C are not mentioned.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Detail: what kind of project do the critics say residents prefer?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph, the second objection ('Second, the process is biased toward the visible').

breakdown.analysis: Find the sentence and paraphrase it. The critics say residents favor 'things they can point to' over replacing water mains. Prephrase: visible projects.

choices.note: Cost never comes up in the critics' objection. Out of scope.
Sounds plausible in real life, but the passage never says it. Don't import outside assumptions.
Council members appear only in the accountability objection, and they don't endorse anything there.
CORRECT. 'Things they can point to' = results residents can readily see.
Reversed. Replacing aging water mains is what residents pass over, according to the critics.

questions.stem: The author mentions the pedestrian crossing near a senior center (last sentence of the second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that residents generally rank safety projects above projects intended to improve a neighborhood’s appearance
suggest that city engineers are, on the whole, less competent than residents at identifying hazards
support the claim that residents’ choices can address needs that the city’s professional planners have missed
illustrate the kind of project the council funds from the remaining 98 percent of the capital budget
give an example of a highly visible project of the kind critics say residents prefer
questions.explanation: The crossing is flagged with 'for example' and illustrates the claim that residents’ projects 'have often addressed problems that city engineers had overlooked,' which is C. B overstates one example into a general comparison of competence, and A turns it into a ranking the passage never gives. E borrows the critics’ point about visible projects, but the author offers the example to rebut that objection, not to illustrate it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Function of an example: why does the author bring up the crossing?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, last sentence: 'the projects residents have chosen have often addressed problems that city engineers had overlooked—a dangerous pedestrian crossing … for example.'

breakdown.analysis: 'For example' tells you exactly what it's an example of: the claim right before the dash. Residents' projects caught problems engineers missed. Prephrase: 'to back up the point that residents spotted needs professionals overlooked.'

choices.note: Too broad. One safety project doesn't show residents 'generally' rank safety first, and the passage draws no such ranking.
Tempting, because engineers missed it. But one missed crossing isn't a judgment about overall competence. Too strong.
CORRECT. The example illustrates the claim that residents' projects 'addressed problems that city engineers had overlooked.'
Wrong budget. The crossing was chosen by residents from the 2 percent set-aside, not funded by the council's 98 percent.
Backwards use. The critics worry about flashy, visible projects; the author uses the crossing to show residents' choices meet real needs.

questions.stem: The author suggests that the officials mentioned in the last sentence of the passage are too
choices: generous
deferential
impatient
sentimental
narrow
questions.explanation: The author says these officials judge the programs by 'the wrong yardstick,' looking only at the size of the sums at stake and ignoring what residents learn. Their standard of value is too narrow, which is E. 'Impatient' (C) may tempt because the officials are dismissive, but nothing suggests they judged too soon.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Single-word completion: what is the author's complaint about the officials?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, last sentence (the 'wrong yardstick' sentence).

breakdown.analysis: What's wrong with their yardstick? They measure only one thing, money, and miss another, learning. That's a too-limited standard. Prephrase: too narrow.

choices.note: Opposite direction. They're dismissive of the programs, not generous toward them.
Nothing suggests they defer to anyone. They're making their own (mistaken) judgment.
Tempting, since dismissing a program can look hasty. But the author's complaint is about what they measure, not how fast they judged.
No support. Their view is hard-headed, if anything, not sentimental.
CORRECT. They count only 'the size of the sums at stake' and ignore 'what residents learn.' That's a narrow measure.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which one of the following was true of Brennick’s participatory budgeting program during its first eight cycles?
choices: Residents of the city’s lowest-income neighborhoods cast a disproportionately large share of the votes.
Proposal meetings were moved from weeknight evenings to times more convenient for most working residents.
Residents were permitted to allocate funds for the repair of water and sewer systems.
The proportion of the capital budget set aside for residents grew after each successful cycle.
The handful of activists who dominate public hearings cast most of the votes on the projects.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the share of votes cast by residents of the lowest-income neighborhoods exceeded those neighborhoods’ share of the population in every cycle, which is A. B is never stated (the passage says nothing about when Brennick’s meetings were held), C contradicts the statement that every dollar for water and sewer systems stays with the council, and E is the skeptics’ failed prediction.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Detail: which statement about Brennick's program does the passage actually state?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, third and fifth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Find the numbers. The share of votes from the lowest-income neighborhoods 'exceeded those neighborhoods' share of the city's population in each of the program's first eight cycles.' More votes than their population share = a disproportionately large share. Prephrase that.

choices.note: CORRECT. Vote share above population share, in every cycle, is a disproportionately large share. Same fact in different words.
Tempting, because it would fix the critics' first objection. But the passage says Brennick changed how ballots were cast, not when meetings were held.
Contradicted. 'Every dollar for water and sewer systems' is still allocated by the council.
Unsupported. The set-aside is 2 percent; nothing says it grew.
That's what the skeptics predicted, and the record 'tells a different story.' Reversed.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the author’s attitude toward participatory budgeting?
choices: skepticism about whether the practice can ever involve a representative group of residents
unqualified enthusiasm for the practice as a solution to each of the problems its critics identify
approval tempered by an acknowledgment that the practice leaves at least one problem unresolved
neutrality, since the author reports the objections and Brennick’s record without evaluating either
reluctant acceptance of a practice that the author regards as largely symbolic
questions.explanation: The author defends the practice (two objections describe avoidable features; it has an overlooked benefit) but concedes that nothing in Brennick’s design addresses accountability. That is approval with a reservation, C. B ignores the concession, D ignores the author’s clear evaluations, and E adopts the 'symbolic' view the author rejects.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Author's attitude toward participatory budgeting.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph: the concession in its first sentence and the favorable conclusions that follow.

breakdown.analysis: Is the author for it or against it? For it: the objections are 'avoidable,' the benefit is real, and the dismissive officials use 'the wrong yardstick.' But there's a 'does not answer every objection' concession. Prephrase: positive, with a reservation. The LSAT loves this attitude; moderate answers usually win.

choices.note: Opposite. The author cites Brennick's turnout as evidence that a representative group can take part.
Too strong. 'Unqualified' and 'each of the problems' ignore the author's concession about accountability.
CORRECT. Favorable overall, with the accountability problem acknowledged as unanswered.
The author evaluates plenty: objections are 'avoidable,' critics 'overlook' a benefit, officials use 'the wrong yardstick.' Not neutral.
The author rejects the 'symbolic' label; that's the officials' view.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about the objection concerning accountability (last sentence of the first paragraph)?
choices: It is the least serious of the three objections, since failed projects are rare under well-designed programs.
It applies just as much to representative government, in which voters also cannot identify whom to remove.
It has been answered by Brennick’s practice of leaving all water and sewer spending to the council.
It would be answered if proposal meetings were scheduled at times convenient for more residents.
It raises a difficulty that Brennick’s program, despite its other successes, has not overcome.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph concedes that 'nothing in its design makes it easier to hold anyone to account for a failed project,' so the author would agree that Brennick has not overcome this difficulty (E). C is the main trap: council control of water and sewer money answers the second objection, about neglected infrastructure, not accountability. A, B, and D make claims the passage never supports.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Author agreement about the third objection (accountability).

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph, last sentence (the objection); third paragraph, first sentence (the author's concession).

breakdown.analysis: Does the author ever answer the accountability point? No. The author admits Brennick's design does nothing for it. So we need an answer that says this objection still stands, at least for Brennick.

choices.note: The author never ranks the objections or says failed projects are rare. Unsupported.
The passage never compares representative government on this point. Out of scope.
Tempting: it's a real fact from the second paragraph. But it answers the second objection (neglected infrastructure), not accountability.
Mixes up objections. Meeting times concern the first objection (who takes part), not accountability.
CORRECT. 'Nothing in its design makes it easier to hold anyone to account for a failed project.' The difficulty remains.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question the author’s suggestion that the first objection described in the first paragraph concerns an avoidable feature of particular programs?
choices: Fewer than one Brennick resident in ten has cast a ballot in any cycle of the program since it began in 2014.
The meetings that draw up Brennick’s ballot have been held on weeknight evenings and attended mostly by residents of its wealthier neighborhoods.
In cities that accept ballots only at public meetings, low-income residents cast a smaller share of votes than in Brennick.
Several of the projects chosen by Brennick’s voters have proved more costly to maintain than city engineers had projected.
Most residents who voted in Brennick’s early cycles had never before attended a public hearing on the city’s budget.
questions.explanation: The first objection is about the proposal meetings that decide which projects appear on the ballot (first paragraph), but Brennick’s evidence concerns only who voted (second paragraph). If even Brennick’s ballot-setting meetings are held on weeknights and dominated by wealthier residents, its design did not avoid the problem, which is B. A is the dominant trap: low turnout sounds like an unrepresentative process, but the author’s evidence is a relative one, the share of votes cast by low-income residents compared with their share of the population, and a small electorate can still have that composition. C and E support the author’s point about voting access, and D concerns cost, not who takes part.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most undermines the author's claim that the first objection (participants aren't a fair sample) describes an avoidable feature, i.e., that Brennick avoided it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, the first objection (it is about 'the proposal meetings at which residents decide which projects will appear on the ballot'); paragraph 2 (Brennick's evidence: votes by mail and at libraries); paragraph 3, second sentence (the 'avoidable features' claim).

breakdown.analysis: What exactly did the critics complain about? Not the vote. The proposal meetings, held on weeknights, that decide what gets on the ballot. And what did Brennick fix? The vote: mail ballots, libraries, grocery stores. So did Brennick avoid the problem the critics described? Only if its meetings were fair too, and the passage never says. We need an answer showing the meetings in Brennick still skew. That answer looks like it just repeats the critics, which is why it hides. Most students pick (A) because low turnout feels like a failure of representation. But the author's evidence is relative: low-income neighborhoods' share of votes exceeds their share of population. That can be true whether 5% or 50% of residents vote. Watch for count-versus-share swaps.

choices.note: Tempting. This is the trap. Low turnout sounds damning, but the author's claim rests on the composition of the voters (share of votes versus share of population), not their number. A small electorate can still be a fair sample.

CORRECT. The objection targets the ballot-setting meetings. If Brennick's are weeknight affairs dominated by wealthier residents, Brennick never avoided the problem; it only widened access to the final vote.
This shows Brennick's voting access works better than the alternative, which supports the author.
Maintenance cost concerns the second objection's territory at most (which projects get chosen), not who participates.
New voters who never attend hearings suggest the activists didn't capture the vote. That supports the author.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Because a rolling easement burdens land that owners never surrendered, the Reyes court sharply limited the circumstances in which the easement may move.
A provincial survey confirmed in every respect Judge Corran’s view that the Ostrander court had misapplied the law of river boundaries to Calder’s coast.
Distinctions drawn from the law of river boundaries cannot sensibly be applied to any coastline, as the experience of Calder’s courts after 1979 demonstrates.
Calder’s speed-based rule for moving the public beach easement drew well-founded criticism and gave way to a persistence test that is easier to apply.
Despite the arbitrariness of its five-year period, the Reyes test has resolved each of the controversies that the Ostrander decision provoked.
questions.explanation: The passage poses the problem, sets out Ostrander’s speed-based rule, presents criticisms that later developments supported, and ends with Reyes’s persistence test and its evidentiary virtue. D captures that arc. A gives the landowners’ objection as Reyes’s motive, which the passage never says; B and E are too extreme ('in every respect,' 'each of the controversies'); C generalizes beyond Calder.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Main point: what is the passage's overall claim?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Whole passage; the conclusion is in the last two sentences of the fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: What's the story here? Problem (the shore moves) → Ostrander's answer (erosion vs. avulsion, i.e., speed) → critics → the 1996 survey 'lent support to these critics' → Reyes replaces speed with persistence, which has 'an evidentiary virtue that Ostrander lacked.' Prephrase: 'the speed test was rightly criticized and replaced by a persistence test that's easier to apply.' The author's measured approval of Reyes is part of the point.

choices.note: Wrong party and wrong motive. That's the landowners' objection; the passage never says it drove Reyes, and Reyes still lets the easement move.
Too strong. The survey 'lent support' to the critics; it didn't confirm Corran's view 'in every respect.'
Too broad. The passage is about Calder, not 'any coastline.'
CORRECT. The speed-based rule drew criticism that later evidence supported, and Reyes's test asks only where the line has stood, a question courts can actually answer.
Too strong. Reyes 'has critics of its own'; nothing says it resolved every controversy.

questions.stem: The author mentions a neighbor who lost the same thirty meters over twenty years (last sentence of the second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: suggest that gradual erosion is more common on Calder’s coast than is sudden loss of land in storms
indicate that the author regards the Ostrander rule as unfair to owners who lose their land gradually
illustrate that the Ostrander rule treats equal losses of land differently depending on how quickly they occurred
show that the Ostrander court misunderstood how the law of river boundaries treats sudden changes
present a case that the test adopted in Reyes would decide differently from the way Ostrander decides it
questions.explanation: The neighbor is paired with the hurricane-struck owner to show a concrete consequence of the rule: identical thirty-meter losses come out differently depending only on speed, which is C. B is tempting, but at this point the author is describing how the rule works, not judging it. E fails because under Reyes a gradual shift that persists five years also moves the easement, so the neighbor’s case comes out the same.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Function of an example: why the neighbor?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, last sentence ('Thus an owner whose dune line retreated thirty meters in one hurricane …').

breakdown.analysis: The sentence starts with 'Thus': it's spelling out what the rule means in practice. Two owners, same thirty meters, one storm vs. twenty years, opposite results. Prephrase: 'to show the rule treats identical losses differently based on speed.'

choices.note: The passage never says which kind of loss is more common; that's the advocates' 'if' in the third paragraph.
Tempting, because the contrast can feel unfair. But the 'Thus' sentence just works out the rule; the author's judgments come later.
CORRECT. Same loss, different result, and the only difference is speed. That's what the pairing shows.
The criticism of the river analogy is Corran's, in the third paragraph. This sentence just applies the rule.
Under Reyes, a gradual shift that persists five years moves the easement too. The neighbor's case comes out the same.

questions.stem: The information in the passage most helps to answer which one of the following questions?
choices: What kind of event did the Ostrander court treat as an example of avulsion?
Why did the Reyes court choose five years, rather than some other period, as its test of persistence?
How many Calder landowners sought compensation from the province after the Ostrander decision?
Did courts in any of Calder’s neighboring provinces adopt the rule announced in Ostrander?
What proportion of the sand fenced after Ostrander was eventually returned to public use?
questions.explanation: The second paragraph defines avulsion as a sudden, perceptible loss 'such as that caused by a single storm,' so A is answerable. B is the trap: the passage mentions critics who call the period arbitrary but never gives the court’s reason. E confuses sand that partly rebuilt on its own (fourth paragraph) with sand returned to public use, and C and D are never addressed.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Answerable question: which question does the passage actually answer?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, second sentence (the definition of avulsion); fourth paragraph for the traps.

breakdown.analysis: Go choice by choice and ask: can I point to a sentence? Most answers here are questions a curious reader would ask that the passage just doesn't address.

choices.note: CORRECT. Avulsion is 'a sudden and perceptible loss such as that caused by a single storm' (second paragraph).
Tempting, since the five-year period is discussed. But the passage only reports that critics call it arbitrary; it never gives the court's reason.
Compensation is never mentioned.
Other provinces' courts are never mentioned.
The survey says fenced sand 'partly rebuilt on its own,' but rebuilt sand isn't the same as sand returned to public use, and no proportion is given.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information in the passage?
choices: Under the Ostrander rule, an owner whose vegetation line retreated gradually could fence the newly exposed sand.
The Reyes court adopted its test chiefly in response to landowners’ complaint that the easement shifted onto land they had never surrendered.
Under the Reyes test, the easement moves to a new vegetation line as soon as the line has shifted.
Judge Corran maintained that the public easement should remain fixed regardless of how the shoreline changes.
Under the Reyes test, the public easement may come to cover sand that was exposed by a single storm.
questions.explanation: Reyes moves the easement whenever a shift has persisted five years, 'however the shift occurred,' so a storm-exposed strip that stays exposed would come under the easement. That is E. A reverses Ostrander, under which only storm-struck owners could fence; C ignores the five-year requirement; B and D read motives and views into the passage that it never states.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Inference: which statement does the passage support?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph (the Reyes test); second paragraph (Ostrander) for the traps.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, but the Reyes test is the obvious place to look: easement moves if the shift persists five years, 'however the shift occurred.' 'However' covers storms. Watch for answers that drop the five-year condition or flip the Ostrander rule.

choices.note: Reversed. Under Ostrander, the easement follows gradual change; it's the storm-struck owner who can fence.
The passage never says why Reyes adopted its test, and Reyes doesn't help landowners on this point anyway: the easement still moves onto their land.
Drops the condition. The easement moves only once the shift 'has persisted for five years.'
Too strong. Corran objected to borrowing the river distinction; she never says the easement should never move.
CORRECT. 'However the shift occurred' includes a storm. If the storm-made line persists five years, the easement moves onto that sand.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the objection to Ostrander raised by public access advocates, as described in the third paragraph?
choices: Many owners of beachfront parcels in Calder bought their land before the courts recognized the public’s customary right.
In the decades after Ostrander, most inland retreat of Calder’s vegetation line occurred in brief storms.
Sand stripped away by a single storm is often partly restored by natural processes over the following months.
The rate of gradual erosion along Calder’s coast increased substantially in the years following the 1979 decision.
Courts in several neighboring provinces have declined to recognize any public right to use privately titled beaches.
questions.explanation: The advocates’ objection rests on a conditional: if most land loss occurs in storms, the avulsion exception would swallow the rule. B confirms the condition, so it strengthens the objection. D points the other way, since more gradual loss means more land over which the easement rolls. C is the geologists’ point and, if anything, suggests some storm losses are temporary; A bears on the landowners’ objection.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Strengthen: what would back up the advocates' objection?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, third sentence (the public access advocates).

breakdown.analysis: The advocates' argument is an if-then: if most loss happens in storms → the storm exception swallows the rule → fences everywhere. So what would strengthen it? Show the 'if' is true. Prephrase: most land loss in fact happens in storms.

choices.note: Bears on the landowners' fairness complaint, not the advocates' worry about fences.
CORRECT. Confirms the 'if' in the advocates' objection: if most retreat came in storms, most newly exposed sand stays private under Ostrander.
This is the geologists' observation, and it cuts against the advocates' fear: storm losses may partly reverse.
Opposite direction. More gradual erosion means more retreat that the easement follows.
Other provinces' law doesn't bear on how Ostrander plays out in Calder.

questions.stem: Which one of the following statements about the test adopted in Reyes v. Port Allard (fourth paragraph) is most strongly supported by the passage?
choices: It answers the landowners’ objection that the easement could move onto land they had never surrendered.
It moves the easement more promptly than the Ostrander rule did in cases of gradual erosion.
It was adopted in response to the 1996 survey’s finding that owners had fenced much of the formerly public dry beach.
It spares courts an inquiry that some scientists who study the coast doubted could be carried out at all.
It prevents landowners from fencing any portion of the sand that a single storm has exposed.
questions.explanation: The coastal geologists doubted that courts could tell gradual retreat from storm loss (third paragraph). Reyes asks only where the vegetation line has stood, ‘not ... how quickly it got there’ (fourth paragraph), so that inquiry drops out, which is D. C is the dominant trap: the survey came before Reyes and ‘lent support’ to the critics, but the passage never says the court acted on it; the sequence is not a stated cause. A fails because the easement still moves onto private land, B has no support (under Reyes a gradual shift must persist five years), and E ignores the five-year wait.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the claim about the Reyes test that the passage actually supports.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3 (the geologists' doubt that the gradual/sudden distinction 'could be applied at all'); paragraph 4 (the survey; Reyes's five-year test; the last sentence on its 'evidentiary virtue').

breakdown.analysis: What does Reyes stop asking? How fast the line moved. Who said that question was unanswerable? The coastal geologists in paragraph 3. Connect those two and you have the answer, but notice that it names the geologists only as 'some scientists who study the coast'. You have to map it back. Most students pick (C) because the survey sits right before Reyes in the same paragraph and the passage says later developments 'lent support' to the critics. But support for the critics isn't a reason the court gave. The passage never says why the court changed course. Order in the paragraph isn't cause.

choices.note: The opposite. Under Reyes the easement still moves onto private land when a shift persists. Landowners' objection to that is untouched.
Nothing supports this. Under Ostrander a gradual shift carried the easement with it; under Reyes it must persist five years first, if anything slower.
Tempting. This is the trap. The survey came first and supported the critics, but the passage never says the Reyes court relied on it. That's a causal claim the passage doesn't make.
CORRECT. The geologists doubted the speed distinction could be applied at all. Reyes asks only where the line has stood for five years, so courts no longer face that inquiry.
Too strong. If the line returns seaward within five years, 'nothing changes', and storm-exposed sand that hasn't persisted for five years stays private in the meantime.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The darkening of Kessin sandpiper eggs toward the north is plausibly explained as an adaptation that limits developmental pauses, despite its cost in concealment.
Valk’s measurements prove that dark eggs cool more slowly than pale ones in every species of shorebird that nests in cold regions.
Kessin sandpiper eggs are darker in the north because the gravel at northern nesting sites is darker than the sand of southern marshes.
In ground-nesting shorebirds, egg color serves mainly to conceal eggs from predators by matching the color of the ground at the nesting site.
Because only the female incubates, the Kessin sandpiper loses more nests to predators than shorebird species in which both parents incubate.
questions.explanation: The passage presents a puzzle (northern eggs are dark despite pale gravel), then Valk’s warming theory, a worked example, and supporting evidence, ending with the author’s qualified endorsement. A states that arc. D is only the general pattern the sandpiper breaks; B overstates ('prove,' 'every species'); C contradicts the statement that northern gravel is pale; E makes a comparison the passage never draws.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Main point: what is the passage's central claim?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Whole passage; the puzzle is at the end of the first paragraph and the verdict in the last sentence of the fourth.

breakdown.analysis: Puzzle → hypothesis → evidence: a classic science passage shape. The puzzle: why are northern eggs dark when that makes them easier to spot? Valk's answer: dark shells keep eggs warmer while the female forages, so development pauses less. The author ends by saying the account turns a 'lapse in camouflage' into a trade-off. Prephrase: 'darkening is plausibly a warmth adaptation that's worth the visibility cost.'

choices.note: CORRECT. Puzzle (darkening despite visibility) plus solution (fewer developmental pauses), with the hedge 'plausibly' matching an account that 'leaves questions open.'
Too strong on two counts: Valk's work 'proves' nothing about 'every species'; it concerns one sandpiper.
Contradicts the passage: northern gravel is pale, which is the whole puzzle.
That's the background rule from the first paragraph that the Kessin sandpiper breaks, not the main point.
The passage never compares nest-loss rates with species where both parents incubate.

questions.stem: According to the passage, at the southern end of the Kessin sandpiper’s range
choices: dark eggs are found by predators more often than dark eggs are in the north
females’ foraging trips are shorter on average than those of females at northern colonies
the species’ eggs are pale enough to match the color of the surrounding sand exactly
air temperatures during the incubation period average roughly 8°C, as at Valk’s northern colony
even pale eggs remain above the developmental threshold for more than an hour
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says that in the south, where the air averages near 20°C, 'even pale eggs took more than an hour to cool to 26°C,' the threshold at which development stops. That is E. C is tempting because southern eggs are paler, but the passage never says they match exactly. D gives the figure for the northern colony, and A and B compare things the passage never measures.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Detail: what does the passage say about the southern end of the range?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Find 'southern end.' One sentence: air near 20°C, and pale eggs take more than an hour to cool to 26°C. 26°C is the threshold from the second paragraph. Prephrase: pale eggs stay warm enough for over an hour.

choices.note: The passage never compares predation on dark eggs in south vs. north.
Foraging-trip length is given only for the northern colony.
Too strong. Eggs get darker toward the north, so southern eggs are paler, but 'match exactly' is never said.
Wrong place. 8°C is the northern colony; the south averages near 20°C.
CORRECT. 'More than an hour to cool to 26°C,' and 26°C is the point where development stops.

questions.stem: By “pays for itself” (last sentence of the second paragraph), Valk most probably means that
choices: producing dark pigment costs the female no more energy than producing pale shells would
dark eggs require the female to spend less total time sitting on the nest during incubation
where the air is cold, dark shells’ protection against developmental delay outweighs their greater visibility
the food the female gathers on her foraging trips supplies the materials needed to darken the shells
dark eggs gradually become harder for predators to see as the breeding season progresses
questions.explanation: Something 'pays for itself' when its benefit outweighs its cost. The benefit is slower cooling and so fewer developmental pauses (second paragraph); the cost is the visibility the first paragraph describes. That is C. A takes 'pays' as a literal energy cost, which the passage never discusses; B confuses shorter incubation with less time on the nest; E contradicts the passage.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Meaning in context: what does 'pays for itself' mean here?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, last sentence; the cost it is weighed against is in the last sentence of the first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Pays for itself compared with what cost? The phrase implies a cost. The first paragraph supplies it: dark eggs are 'especially easy to spot' on pale gravel. The benefit is in the second paragraph: less cooling, fewer pauses, fewer days at risk. Prephrase: 'in cold places, the warmth benefit outweighs the visibility cost.' The trap is the literal, dictionary reading of 'pays.'

choices.note: Takes 'pays' literally, as a metabolic cost. The passage never discusses the energy cost of pigment.
Tempting, since fewer pauses shorten incubation. But that's about days until hatching, not time sitting on the nest, and it skips the cost side of the trade-off.
CORRECT. Benefit (fewer developmental pauses) outweighs cost (easier to spot), and only where the air is cold.
Invented mechanism. Nothing links foraging to pigment.
Contradicts the passage: dark eggs stay easier to spot ('day for day, darker clutches were found by predators somewhat more often').

questions.stem: The author mentions the two colonies “lying at the same latitude” (fourth paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: suggest that egg predators are more numerous on wind-scoured islands than in sheltered inland valleys
provide the temperature figures that are used in the worked example in the third paragraph
identify a case that Valk’s theory, by the author’s own admission, has not yet explained
show that egg darkness tracks the variable Valk’s theory emphasizes rather than mere geographic position
indicate that females at island colonies take longer foraging trips than females at inland colonies
questions.explanation: Two colonies at the same latitude but with different temperatures lay eggs of different darkness, which shows that darkness tracks breeding-season temperature, the variable Valk’s theory depends on, rather than position on the map. That is D. C is tempting because the paragraph does mention an open question, but that question concerns pale clutches among northern neighbors, not these colonies. A and E invent differences the passage never mentions, and B misplaces the example.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Function of an example: why the two same-latitude colonies?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The sentence opens with its own claim: darkness 'tracks breeding-season temperature more closely than it tracks latitude.' The two colonies prove it: same latitude, colder island, darker eggs. Why does that matter? Temperature is what Valk's theory runs on. Prephrase: 'to show darkness follows temperature, as the theory predicts, not just location.'

choices.note: Predator numbers aren't discussed for these colonies.
The worked example uses figures from a different (northern) colony. No temperatures are given for these two.
Tempting: the paragraph does admit an open question. But that's about some northern females laying paler clutches, not these two colonies.
CORRECT. Same latitude, different temperature, different darkness: darkness tracks temperature, the variable Valk's mechanism depends on.
Foraging-trip lengths for these colonies are never given.

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward Valk’s theory can most accurately be described as
choices: skepticism about the physical mechanism on which the theory relies
favorable regard tempered by acknowledgment that some questions remain open
unreserved enthusiasm for a theory regarded as having settled the matter
reluctant acceptance of a theory that conflicts with established experimental findings
detached neutrality between the theory and the concealment view it challenges
questions.explanation: The author says two observations 'support Valk’s account' and credits it with turning an apparent lapse into a predictable result, while noting that it 'leaves questions open.' That mix is B. C ignores the caveat. D is tempting, but the author shows no reluctance, and the theory accepts rather than conflicts with the finding that matched eggs are better concealed. A and E do not fit the author’s supportive language.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Author's attitude toward Valk's theory.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, first and last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The author says observations 'support Valk's account' and ends by crediting the account with turning a 'lapse in camouflage' into a predictable trade-off, but also says it 'leaves questions open.' Prephrase: positive with a reservation.

choices.note: The author never questions that dark shells absorb more sunlight; the evidence is presented as support.
CORRECT. 'Support Valk's account' plus 'leaves questions open' = favorable, with a reservation.
Too strong. 'Unreserved' ignores the open questions.
No reluctance, and no conflict: the theory grants that dark eggs are easier to find and argues the warmth benefit outweighs that.
The author isn't neutral: 'support' and the closing sentence take a side.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question Valk’s theory as described in the second paragraph?
choices: At northern colonies, predators find dark clutches more often, day for day, than they find pale clutches at the same sites.
Females at southern colonies take foraging trips that are, on average, somewhat longer than those of northern females.
Several shorebird species that nest alongside the Kessin sandpiper in the north lay pale eggs, and in those species both parents incubate.
The pigment that darkens Kessin sandpiper eggs requires the female to expend energy that she must replace by foraging.
Among northern colonies, eggs are no darker where skies are usually clear during incubation than where they are mostly overcast.
questions.explanation: Valk’s mechanism is that dark shells ‘absorb more sunlight’ and so cool more slowly, and the worked example concerns eggs ‘exposed to sunlight.’ If eggs are just as dark where there is little sun to absorb, the trait does not track the benefit said to explain it, so E undermines the theory. A is the dominant trap: it attacks a cost the theory already concedes; the fourth paragraph reports that darker clutches were found by predators more often, day for day, and still hatched more often overall. C fits the theory, since eggs with two incubating parents are seldom left uncovered; B and D do not touch the trade-off.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most damages Valk's claim that dark eggs are an adaptation for warmth.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2 (the mechanism: dark shells 'absorb more sunlight'); paragraph 3 (the example uses eggs 'exposed to sunlight'); paragraph 4 (darker clutches found more often by predators, yet hatch more often).

breakdown.analysis: Where does the warmth come from in Valk's story? Sunlight. Dark shells soak up sun, so they cool slowly. So what should happen where there's little sun? Darkness should buy less, and if the theory is right, eggs there should be less dark. A finding that darkness ignores cloud cover cuts the trait loose from its supposed benefit. Most students pick (A) because 'dark eggs get eaten more' sounds like the obvious objection to a dark-egg adaptation. But the passage already grants it. Valk's account is a trade-off: more predation day for day, fewer days in the nest. Attacking a cost the argument concedes doesn't weaken it.

choices.note: Tempting. This is the trap. The passage already concedes this: darker clutches 'were found by predators somewhat more often' day for day, yet hatched more often overall. A theory built on a trade-off isn't hurt by its admitted cost.
Southern pale eggs take over an hour to cool to the threshold. Somewhat longer trips there still wouldn't make darkening pay. No effect.
Fits the theory. With two parents, eggs are rarely left uncovered, so there's no cooling problem to solve.
Every trait has some cost. This doesn't show the warmth benefit is missing or too small.
CORRECT. The benefit depends on absorbing sunlight. If eggs are no darker where skies are clear than where they are overcast, darkness doesn't track the factor that supposedly makes it pay.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information in the passage?
choices: Kessin sandpiper eggs are darkest at whichever colonies lie farthest north, where pale gravel makes them easiest to spot.
Over a full incubation at the northern colony Valk studied, the embryo in a dark egg would never have its development halted.
Kessin sandpiper eggs that are left uncovered in cold air for more than about 15 minutes generally fail to hatch.
If females at Valk’s northern colony typically returned to the nest within about 15 minutes, dark eggs there would offer little developmental advantage.
At the southern end of the range, females spend less time away from the nest each day than northern females do.
questions.explanation: At the northern colony a pale egg takes about 15 minutes to cool to the 26°C threshold. If trips were usually no longer than that, pale eggs would rarely reach the threshold, so dark shells would gain little developmental time, which is D. A is the dominant trap: eggs do darken toward the north, but the fourth paragraph says darkness tracks breeding-season temperature more closely than latitude, so the farthest-north colony need not be the darkest. B is too strong, because dark eggs avoid a pause only ‘on most trips’; C confuses a halt in development with failure to hatch; E compares something the passage never measures.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the passage's facts actually support. The numbers in paragraph 3 are the place to work.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3 (pale egg: 15 minutes to the threshold; trips about 25 minutes; dark egg: about 28 minutes, 'on most trips' no pause); paragraph 4, first observation (darkness tracks temperature more than latitude).

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, so run the numbers. A pale egg hits 26°C in about 15 minutes. The trips last about 25, so the pale egg spends about 10 minutes stalled. Dark eggs take about 28, so they usually don't stall. The whole advantage lives in the gap between 15 minutes and the length of the trip. Shrink the trip below 15 and pale eggs never stall either: no advantage left. That's (D), stated as a hypothetical. Most students pick (A) because paragraph 1 says eggs 'grow steadily darker toward the north'. But paragraph 4 says darkness tracks temperature 'more closely than it tracks latitude', and the island colony shows a colder site beating a warmer one at the same latitude. 'Farthest north' isn't 'coldest'. One word, different variable.

choices.note: Tempting. This is the trap. The trend runs north, but paragraph 4 says darkness tracks temperature more closely than latitude. The darkest eggs would be at the coldest colonies, which need not be the northernmost.
Too strong. Dark eggs avoid a pause only 'on most trips'. 'Never' overshoots.
Halted development isn't death. The passage says the embryo 'stops developing until it is warmed again', not that it fails.
CORRECT. The pale egg's 15-minute cooling time is the threshold. Trips shorter than that leave pale eggs above 26°C, so darkness buys little time.
The passage gives southern temperatures and cooling times but says nothing about how long southern females are away.

questions.stimulus: Last spring the city installed brighter lamps along the walking paths in Fenwick Park. During the following summer, the park had nearly twice as many evening visitors as it had had the summer before. Clearly, then, it was the brighter lamps that drew the additional visitors to the park after dark.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: presumes that what is true of Fenwick Park must also be true of every other park in the city
relies on visitor counts that may have been gathered by people who favored the new lamps
takes for granted that the lamps were installed in response to complaints from visitors about the dark
overlooks the possibility that some change other than the new lamps could account for the increase in evening visitors
fails to establish that the additional visitors stayed in the park longer than earlier visitors did
questions.explanation: The argument infers that the lamps caused the rise in evening visitors simply because the rise followed their installation, ignoring other possible causes such as a new event, warmer weather, or new nearby housing; D names this. A is tempting because such arguments often overgeneralize, but this one draws no conclusion about any other park. B, C, and E describe assumptions the argument never makes or needs.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The brighter lamps are what drew the extra evening visitors to Fenwick Park.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Brighter lamps went in last spring; the following summer, evening visitors nearly doubled.

breakdown.analysis: Classic 'it came after, so it caused it' reasoning. The arguer sees two things happen in sequence and declares one the cause of the other. But lots of things change from one summer to the next: weather, events, new housing nearby, a popular food truck. It's like saying: I started wearing my lucky socks in March and my team won more games in April, so the socks won the games. Prephrase: the argument ignores other possible causes of the jump in visitors.

choices.note: Wrong. This describes an overgeneralization from one park to all parks. The argument never says a word about any other park. Tempting only because overgeneralizing is a common flaw.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Brighter lamps boosted visits at Fenwick Park, so brighter lamps will boost visits at every park in the city.

choices.note: Wrong. This is a biased-source attack. Nothing in the stimulus says who counted visitors or that they had a stake in the lamps. You can't pick an answer on a possibility the stimulus never raises.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The lamp company's own staff counted twice as many visitors, so the lamps clearly worked.

choices.note: Wrong. Why the lamps were installed doesn't matter to whether they caused more visits. The argument makes no assumption about complaints.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The city installed lamps, so residents must have been complaining about the dark.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the textbook causal flaw. The rise in visitors followed the lamps, but something else (a new event, nicer weather, new apartments nearby) could explain it. The argument never rules those out.
Wrong. The conclusion is about drawing more visitors, not about how long they stayed. The argument doesn't need visit length at all. The LSAT is ultra specific: this is about the number of visitors.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The lamps made the park more enjoyable, since more people came, so people must be staying longer.

questions.stimulus: Theater critic: The Harrow Playhouse should not abandon its practice of staging one new play by a local writer each season. Admittedly, these productions sell fewer tickets than the playhouse's revivals of familiar classics. But several plays that premiered at the Harrow have gone on to successful runs elsewhere, and that reputation for discovery is a major reason donors continue to support the playhouse.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the conclusion drawn in the argument?
choices: The Harrow Playhouse should continue staging one new play by a local writer each season.
The Harrow's productions of new local plays sell fewer tickets than its revivals of classics.
Several plays that premiered at the Harrow Playhouse have gone on to successful runs elsewhere.
Donors support the Harrow Playhouse mainly because of its reputation for discovering new plays.
The Harrow Playhouse should stage more new plays and fewer revivals of familiar classics.
questions.explanation: The first sentence is the conclusion: the playhouse should keep its practice of one new local play per season, and the rest of the stimulus concedes a cost and then gives reasons for keeping it, so A is correct. D distorts a premise (the critic says the reputation is 'a major reason,' not the main one), B is the conceded point, and E goes further than the critic, who argues only for keeping the current practice.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Harrow Playhouse should not abandon staging one new local play each season.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Concession: new plays sell fewer tickets than revivals; but several Harrow premieres succeeded elsewhere; that reputation for discovery is a major reason donors keep giving.

breakdown.analysis: The structure is conclusion first, then 'Admittedly...' (a concession), then 'But...' (the reasons). The concession and the reasons all serve the opening sentence. Quick test: ask 'why?' after each sentence. Why shouldn't they abandon it? Because of the reputation and the donors. That tells you the first sentence is the point. Prephrase: keep doing the one-new-local-play-a-year thing.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Should not abandon' the practice is the same as 'should continue' it. This is just the first sentence, restated.
Wrong. This is the concession, introduced by 'Admittedly.' The critic grants it and then argues past it. A conceded point is never the conclusion.
Wrong. This is a premise. It's offered as support for why the practice is worth keeping.
