Wrong. It distorts a premise. The critic says the reputation is 'a major reason' donors give, not the main reason. Watch the switch from 'a major' to 'mainly.' And even accurately stated, it's support, not the conclusion.
Wrong. Too strong. The critic only argues for keeping the current practice of one new play per season, not for adding more new plays or cutting revivals.

questions.stimulus:
Ruiz: The Brookfield Public Library's main branch should stay open until 10 p.m. on weekdays. Many residents work until 6 p.m. or later, and the current 7 p.m. closing time leaves them almost no chance to use the library during the week.

Okafor: The library's budget is fixed, so longer hours would mean buying fewer new books. Residents who work late can still visit on Saturdays, and most of what the library offers is available online at any hour.
questions.stem: Ruiz and Okafor disagree over whether
choices: many Brookfield residents work until 6 p.m. or later
most of the library's offerings can be used online at any hour
the library's main branch should stay open until 10 p.m. on weekdays
residents who work late are able to visit the library on Saturdays
the library's budget should be increased to pay for keeping the main branch open longer
questions.explanation: Ruiz proposes the later weekday closing, and Okafor gives reasons against adopting it (fewer books, and other ways to use the library), so they disagree about C. Okafor never disputes that many residents work late (A), and Ruiz says nothing about online offerings (B) or Saturday visits (D); D is tempting because Okafor raises it, but Ruiz's complaint is specifically about weekdays. Neither proposes a larger budget (E).

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ruiz: The main branch should stay open until 10 p.m. on weekdays because many residents work until 6 or later and can't get there before 7; Okafor: Longer hours would cost new books, late workers can come Saturdays, and most offerings are online.

breakdown.analysis: Okafor never says 'no' in so many words, but every point is a reason against the later hours. Ruiz proposes; Okafor rebuts. To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. On the 10 p.m. weekday closing, Ruiz says yes and Okafor clearly says no. Prephrase: whether the library should stay open later on weekdays.

choices.note: Wrong. Ruiz says it, but Okafor never disputes it. In fact Okafor talks about 'residents who work late' as if they exist. No disagreement.
Wrong. Only Okafor talks about online offerings. Ruiz has no stated view, so you can't say they disagree.
CORRECT. Ruiz explicitly says the branch should stay open until 10 p.m. on weekdays. Okafor's whole response is a set of reasons not to do it. Yes versus no.

Wrong. Tempting because Okafor raises Saturdays as a response. But Ruiz's complaint is specifically about weekdays and never says late workers can't come on Saturday. Ruiz has no stated position here.
Wrong. Neither speaker proposes raising the budget. Okafor treats the budget as fixed, and Ruiz never mentions it.

questions.stimulus: Nutritionist: In a survey of 400 office workers, those who said they ate breakfast every day reported feeling noticeably more alert during morning meetings than did those who said they usually skipped breakfast. Hence, eating breakfast increases a person's alertness in the morning.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the nutritionist's argument?
choices: Many of the office workers surveyed said that they drank coffee during their morning meetings.
Most of the surveyed workers who usually skipped breakfast also reported getting far less sleep than the breakfast eaters.
Some foods commonly eaten at breakfast contain more sugar than most nutritionists recommend that adults consume.
A few of the surveyed workers who ate breakfast every day reported feeling tired and distracted during their afternoon meetings at work.
Office workers who usually skip breakfast tend to eat a noticeably larger lunch than office workers who eat breakfast.
questions.explanation: The argument moves from a correlation to the claim that breakfast causes alertness. B offers an alternative cause: the breakfast skippers also sleep much less, which could explain their lower alertness. A would matter only if coffee drinking differed between the two groups, which it does not say; D concerns afternoons, and E concerns lunch.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Eating breakfast increases a person's morning alertness.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In a survey, office workers who ate breakfast daily reported feeling more alert in morning meetings than those who usually skipped it.

breakdown.analysis: Correlation to causation. Breakfast eaters feel more alert, so breakfast causes alertness. To weaken, find something else that differs between the two groups and could explain the alertness gap. Prephrase: the breakfast eaters differ in some other way, like sleep or overall health habits. It's like saying people who own running shoes are fitter, so buying running shoes makes you fit.

choices.note: Wrong. Coffee would matter only if one group drank more of it than the other. 'Many' of all workers drank coffee tells you nothing about a difference between the groups.
CORRECT. Alternative cause. The breakfast skippers also slept far less. Lack of sleep could easily explain why they felt less alert, with breakfast doing nothing at all.
Wrong. Sugar content and nutritionists' recommendations have nothing to do with whether breakfast affects alertness.
Wrong. The conclusion is about morning alertness. 'A few' breakfast eaters feeling tired in the afternoon is the wrong time of day and too small a group to matter.
Wrong. Lunch size doesn't bear on morning alertness, since lunch comes after the morning meetings.

questions.stimulus: Ornithologists studying marsh wrens in the Teller Wetlands found that each male builds several dummy nests in addition to the nest in which eggs are laid. Building these extra nests costs the birds considerable time and energy. Yet wrens that build more dummy nests tend to raise more chicks than wrens that build fewer.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain how building dummy nests could increase the number of chicks a wren raises?
choices: Predators that find an empty dummy nest often stop searching the area before finding the nest with eggs.
Dummy nests are usually built from the same materials as the nests that hold eggs.
Wrens in the Teller Wetlands build more dummy nests in years when the insects they feed their chicks are plentiful.
Some other bird species in the Teller Wetlands also build nests that they never use.
Female wrens typically lay the same number of eggs regardless of how many nests the male has built.
questions.explanation: The stem asks how building dummy nests could itself lead to more chicks. A supplies a mechanism: dummy nests divert predators, so more eggs and chicks survive. C is the attractive trap, but it offers a different cause (plentiful food), suggesting the link is not causal, rather than explaining how the nests help; E, if anything, rules out one possible mechanism.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Building dummy nests costs male wrens a lot of time and energy, but wrens that build more dummy nests raise more chicks.

breakdown.analysis: The stem is specific: explain HOW building dummy nests could increase the number of chicks. So you need a mechanism where the dummy nests themselves help chicks survive or get produced. Prephrase: the dummy nests protect the real nest somehow (decoys), or they attract more mates. Think of a shell game: put the prize under one of five cups and a thief has worse odds than if there's only one cup.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the mechanism. Predators find an empty decoy, give up, and the real nest survives. More dummy nests means more decoys, so more eggs make it and more chicks get raised. The cost is worth it.
Wrong. Irrelevant. What the nests are made of says nothing about why more of them means more chicks.

Wrong. This is the trap. It offers a different cause, plentiful food, that drives both nest-building and chick-raising. That suggests the nests don't cause anything. The stem asks how the nests themselves could help, so an alternative cause doesn't answer it.
Wrong. Other species doing something similar doesn't explain how it helps wrens raise chicks. Out of scope.
Wrong. If anything, this rules out one possible mechanism (more nests → more eggs). It doesn't explain how the nests lead to more chicks.

questions.stimulus: A panel of professional chefs tasted each of the twelve sauces that the Mirela Bistro has developed for its new menu and rated every one of them excellent. Each dish on the new menu will combine one of these sauces with a main ingredient that the bistro already prepares superbly. So every dish on the new menu will be excellent.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: fails to consider whether diners will pay more for the dishes on the new menu than for the old ones
relies on the ratings of chefs who may have had a hand in developing the sauces they were asked to judge
draws a conclusion about all of the new sauces from a tasting of only some of them
treats the success of the bistro's current dishes as proof that its new menu will be equally popular
takes for granted that combining elements that are each excellent on their own will produce something excellent
questions.explanation: The argument moves from the excellence of each component (every sauce, every main ingredient) to the excellence of every combination, but two excellent components can still make a poor dish; E names this part-to-whole assumption. B is tempting because biased judges are a familiar flaw, but nothing suggests the chefs helped develop the sauces. C misdescribes the tasting, which covered all twelve sauces, and A and D raise price and popularity, which the conclusion never mentions.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Every dish on the bistro's new menu will be excellent.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: All twelve new sauces were rated excellent; each dish pairs one of those sauces with a main ingredient the bistro already prepares superbly.

breakdown.analysis: So what if every part is excellent? Great parts don't guarantee a great whole. A superb sauce can clash with a superb piece of fish. It's like arguing: every player on this team is an all-star, so the team will be great. Maybe, but they still have to play well together. This is the part-to-whole flaw (composition). It's a classic; know it. Prephrase: the argument assumes that excellent components automatically make an excellent combination.

choices.note: Wrong. Price is a different dimension. The conclusion is about whether the dishes will be excellent, not whether diners will pay for them.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The new dishes are excellent, so diners will gladly pay twice as much for them.

choices.note: Tempting, because biased judges are a real flaw. But nothing says the chefs had any role in developing the sauces. You can't pick an answer on a possibility the stimulus never raises.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The sauces must be excellent, since the chefs who invented them all rated them highly.

choices.note: Wrong. The panel tasted each of the twelve sauces. There's no sample here; every sauce was tested.
choices.example: Example of flaw: We tasted three of the twelve sauces and liked them, so all twelve must be excellent.

choices.note: Wrong. The argument never mentions popularity or the current menu's success. It's about quality, and it relies on the main ingredients being prepared superbly, not on past sales.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our old menu sold well, so our new menu will sell just as well.

choices.note: CORRECT. The argument goes from 'each sauce is excellent' and 'each ingredient is prepared superbly' to 'each combination is excellent.' That skips whether the pieces work together.

questions.stimulus: Last year the Coralton Water Authority began sending some of its customers monthly reports comparing their water use with that of similar nearby households. Over the following year, customers who received the reports used 4 percent less water than they had the year before. The authority concludes that the reports led those customers to reduce their water use.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the authority's argument?
choices: Water rates in Coralton's service area rose noticeably during the year in which the reports were first being sent out.
Many of the customers who received the reports said that they found the comparisons in them confusing or hard to interpret.
Customers randomly chosen not to receive the reports used about as much water as they had the year before.
Several other water utilities in the region have recently begun sending similar comparison reports to their own customers.
On average, customers who received the reports used more water than the similar households they were compared with.
questions.explanation: The argument attributes a drop in use to the reports, so it is vulnerable to other causes that would have reduced everyone's use. C supplies a control group: comparable customers without reports did not cut back, which makes the reports the likely cause. A is a trap that actually weakens by offering an alternative cause (higher water rates), and D and E do not bear on whether the reports caused the drop.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The comparison reports led customers to cut their water use.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Customers who got the reports used 4 percent less water than the year before.

breakdown.analysis: Another causal argument with no comparison. Maybe everyone used less last year, thanks to mild weather, rate hikes, or new water-saving fixtures. To strengthen, rule out those alternatives. Best tool: a control group. If similar customers who didn't get reports didn't cut back, the reports look like the cause. Prephrase: customers without reports didn't reduce their use.

choices.note: Wrong. This is a trap that weakens. Higher water rates are an alternative reason customers would use less water, reports or not.
Wrong. If anything, confusing reports make it less likely they changed behavior. Doesn't strengthen.

CORRECT. A random control group. Customers randomly kept from getting reports used about the same as before, so whatever changed last year wasn't pushing everyone down. That points to the reports as the cause of the 4 percent drop.
Wrong. What other utilities are doing tells you nothing about whether Coralton's reports worked.
Wrong. Knowing they started out above their neighbors might suggest a motive to cut back, but it doesn't show the reports actually caused the drop. Other causes are still on the table.

questions.stimulus: Geologist: A layer of volcanic ash in the cliffs above Maren Bay matches, in chemical composition, the ash produced by an eruption of Mount Askel about 9,000 years ago. The ash from a given eruption has a chemical signature that distinguishes it from the ash of most other eruptions. Therefore, the sediment layers lying directly beneath this ash in the cliffs were deposited more than about 9,000 years ago.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the geologist's argument?
choices: The eruption of Mount Askel was the largest eruption in the region in the last 9,000 years.
Ash from the Mount Askel eruption can be found at many sites besides Maren Bay.
No eruption much more recent than 9,000 years ago produced ash chemically identical to the Askel ash.
The sediment layers beneath the ash at Maren Bay were deposited at a steady rate.
Volcanic ash is the most reliable means geologists have for dating sediment layers.
questions.explanation: The argument dates the ash layer by its chemical match to the Askel eruption, so it requires that the match not have some other, later source. Negate C: if a much later eruption produced identical ash, the layer could be far younger, and the dating collapses. A is the tempting trap because size seems to matter, but the eruption need not be the largest for the match to identify it; B, D, and E are not needed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The sediment layers directly beneath the ash in the Maren Bay cliffs were deposited more than about 9,000 years ago.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The ash layer matches, chemically, the ash from Mount Askel's eruption about 9,000 years ago; layers below are older than layers above.

breakdown.analysis: The geologist dates the ash by matching it to Askel's eruption. That only works if the match actually pins the ash to that eruption. If some other, later eruption could produce the same chemical fingerprint, the ash could be much younger and so could the layers under it. It's like identifying someone by a fingerprint: you're assuming nobody else has the same print. Prephrase: no other, later source produced matching ash.

choices.note: Wrong. Not needed. The eruption doesn't have to be the biggest for its ash to be identified by chemistry. Negating it doesn't hurt the argument. Tempting because size feels like it should matter.
choices.negation: The Mount Askel eruption was not the largest eruption in the region in the last 9,000 years.

choices.note: Wrong. Whether Askel ash shows up elsewhere doesn't affect dating the layer at Maren Bay. Negating it does no harm.
choices.negation: Ash from the Mount Askel eruption cannot be found at many sites besides Maren Bay.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it and the argument falls apart: if a much more recent eruption produced chemically identical ash, then the ash at Maren Bay might come from that eruption, and the layers beneath could be much younger than 9,000 years.
choices.negation: Some eruption much more recent than 9,000 years ago produced ash chemically identical to the Askel ash.

choices.note: Wrong. Deposit rate would matter if you were calculating how old a layer is from its thickness. The argument only claims the layers under the ash are older than the ash. Uneven deposition doesn't change that. Negating it doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: The sediment layers beneath the ash were not deposited at a steady rate.

choices.note: Wrong. Too strong. The method just has to work here, not be the most reliable method there is. Negating it doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: Volcanic ash is not the most reliable means geologists have for dating sediment layers.

questions.stimulus: This year Westbrook Elementary School began setting out bowls of free fruit in its cafeteria at lunch. Since then, its students have, on average, been eating noticeably fewer cookies and chips at lunch than they did last year. Clearly, then, offering free fruit leads children to eat fruit in place of snack foods.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions most helps in evaluating the argument?
choices: Do Westbrook students prefer some kinds of fruit, such as apples, to other kinds offered at lunch?
How much does it cost Westbrook each year to provide free fruit to students at lunch?
Is fruit generally more nutritious for growing children than cookies, chips, and other packaged snack foods are?
Did students at comparable schools without free fruit also eat fewer cookies and chips at lunch this year?
Do Westbrook students eat more cookies and chips at home after school than they did last year?
questions.explanation: The argument credits the fruit program for a drop in snack eating, so the key question is whether something else, such as a district-wide change, caused the drop. If comparable schools without free fruit saw the same decline, the program looks irrelevant; if not, the argument is strengthened, so D is useful either way. E is tempting, but the conclusion concerns what children eat at lunch, not at home, and A, B, and C do not bear on the causal claim.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Offering free fruit leads children to eat fruit in place of snack foods.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Westbrook began offering free fruit at lunch this year, and its students now eat fewer cookies and chips at lunch than last year.

breakdown.analysis: Causal claim from a before-and-after change at one school. Maybe something else cut snack eating, like a district snack ban or price hike. The useful question checks for that: did similar schools without fruit see the same drop? If yes, the fruit looks irrelevant. If no, the fruit looks like the cause. Either answer moves the argument, which is what an evaluate answer needs.

choices.note: Wrong. Which fruit they like best doesn't affect whether the fruit program caused the drop in snacks.
Wrong. Cost has nothing to do with whether the fruit caused the change. The LSAT is ultra specific: this is about cause, not cost.
Wrong. Nutrition is beside the point. The argument is about what kids eat, not whether it's good for them.

CORRECT. A control-group question. If comparable schools without free fruit also saw snack eating drop, something else is the likely cause and the argument weakens. If they didn't, the fruit looks responsible and the argument strengthens.
Wrong. Tempting, but the conclusion is about eating fruit in place of snacks at lunch. What kids eat at home after school doesn't test that.

questions.stimulus: Gray shrikes in the Ostrava Hills impale the insects they catch on thorns before eating them. One grasshopper species common in the hills carries a toxin that breaks down within two days after the insect dies. Shrikes eat most impaled prey within a few hours, but they leave impaled grasshoppers of this species on the thorns for two days or more before eating them. Thus, ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: shrikes impale prey on thorns chiefly in order to make toxic prey safe to eat
the toxin carried by these grasshoppers is harmful to most of the bird species that eat them
shrikes would eat more of these grasshoppers if the grasshoppers' toxin broke down more quickly
shrikes in the Ostrava Hills catch more of these grasshoppers than any other kind of prey
the shrikes' practice of impaling prey may help protect them from the grasshoppers' toxin
questions.explanation: Shrikes wait just long enough for the toxin to break down before eating these grasshoppers, so impaling, which lets them store the prey, plausibly protects them from the toxin, as E cautiously states. A overreaches with 'chiefly': shrikes impale all their prey, most of which they eat within hours, so detoxifying cannot be the main purpose. B, C, and D go beyond anything the facts establish.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Shrikes impale insects they catch on thorns before eating them; 2) One common grasshopper carries a toxin that breaks down within two days after it dies; 3) Shrikes eat most impaled prey within hours; 4) They leave these grasshoppers impaled for two days or more before eating them.

breakdown.analysis: The facts line up suspiciously well: the toxin breaks down in two days, and shrikes wait two days or more before eating these grasshoppers. So impaling gives them a way to store the toxic prey until it's safe. That's the inference. But careful: shrikes impale everything, and eat most prey within hours, so detox can't be the main reason they impale. Prephrase: impaling may help shrikes avoid the toxin.

choices.note: Wrong. Too strong with 'chiefly.' Shrikes impale all their prey and eat most of it within a few hours, so detoxifying can't be the main purpose. It's one benefit for one species of prey.
Wrong. The facts are only about shrikes and this grasshopper. Nothing tells you about most bird species.
Wrong. Unsupported prediction. Nothing says shrikes are limited by the wait. They might eat exactly as many either way.
Wrong. Nothing about how much of their diet is grasshoppers. 'Common in the hills' isn't 'most-caught prey.'

CORRECT. The hedge ('may help') makes it easy to support. The waiting time matches the toxin's breakdown time, and impaling is what lets them store prey that long. So impaling plausibly protects them from the toxin.

questions.stimulus: Energy analyst: Ten years ago, rooftop solar panels generated 5 percent of the electricity used by households in Velmont. Today they generate 9 percent, and the share supplied by all other sources combined has fallen accordingly. So Velmont households now draw less electricity from sources other than rooftop solar than they did ten years ago.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the energy analyst's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: fails to consider that a smaller percentage of a larger total can exceed a larger percentage of a smaller total
takes for granted that a trend observed over the past decade will continue at the same pace into the next
presumes, without providing justification, that rooftop solar panels are less costly than other sources of electricity
treats evidence about electricity used by households as though it applied to businesses as well
fails to consider whether households in neighboring towns have seen a similar rise in the share of electricity supplied by solar
questions.explanation: The non-solar share fell from 95 to 91 percent, but if total household use rose by more than about 4.4 percent, the amount drawn from non-solar sources actually increased; A describes this percent-versus-amount error. B is tempting, but the conclusion is about the present, not a prediction. D describes a confusion the argument never makes, since it concerns only households, and C and E raise matters the conclusion does not depend on.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Velmont households now use less electricity from non-solar sources than ten years ago.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Rooftop solar's share of household electricity rose from 5 percent to 9 percent.

breakdown.analysis: The analyst goes from percentages to amounts. Non-solar's share dropped from 95 to 91 percent, but a smaller slice of a bigger pie can be more pie. Worked example: ten years ago households used 100 units, 95 non-solar. Today they use 120 units; 91 percent of 120 is about 109 non-solar units. That's more, not less. Prephrase: the argument ignores that total use may have grown.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the percent-versus-amount error. If total household use grew by more than about 4.4 percent, 91 percent of the new total exceeds 95 percent of the old one, so non-solar use actually went up.
Wrong. The conclusion is about now versus ten years ago, not a prediction about the next decade. Tempting because 'trend' sounds right, but there's no forecast here.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Solar's share grew 4 points over the last decade, so it will be at 13 percent ten years from now.

choices.note: Wrong. Cost never comes up. The conclusion is about how much non-solar electricity is used, and the argument doesn't depend on solar being cheaper.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Households are switching to solar, so solar must be the cheaper option.

choices.note: Wrong. The argument talks only about households, start to finish. It never extends anything to businesses.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Households now get 9 percent of their power from solar, so Velmont businesses must too.

choices.note: Wrong. Other towns are irrelevant. The conclusion is only about Velmont, and what happened elsewhere wouldn't fix or reveal the percent problem.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Velmont's solar share rose, so solar's share must be rising in every neighboring town too.

questions.stimulus: Principal: Some teachers doubt that our new humanities courses belong in the information-literacy requirement. But any course that requires students to complete a substantial independent research project develops students' ability to evaluate sources. Every course in Fairview High School's new humanities sequence requires such a project. Therefore, every course in the new humanities sequence should count toward the school's information-literacy requirement.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the principal's argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Only courses that develop students' ability to evaluate sources should be counted toward the school's information-literacy requirement.
Any course that develops students' ability to evaluate sources should count toward the school's information-literacy requirement.
Students who complete a substantial independent research project tend to evaluate sources better than students who do not complete one.
Every course that counts toward the information-literacy requirement requires a substantial independent research project.
Most of the courses offered outside the new humanities sequence do not develop students' ability to evaluate sources.
questions.explanation: The premises establish that every course in the sequence develops students' ability to evaluate sources; B links that property to counting toward the requirement, so the conclusion follows. A is the attractive trap but reverses the needed conditional: it makes source evaluation necessary for counting, not sufficient. D likewise reverses direction, and C and E do not connect the courses to the requirement.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Every course in the new humanities sequence should count toward the information-literacy requirement.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Substantial research project → develops source evaluation; every course in the sequence requires such a project.

breakdown.analysis: Map the chain. Humanities sequence course → research project → develops source evaluation. The conclusion jumps to → should count toward info-literacy. The missing link: develops source evaluation → should count. Full chain: sequence course → research project → source evaluation → counts. Like: all my roommates are nurses, all nurses work nights, so my roommates should get the night-shift discount. You need 'night workers get the discount.'

choices.note: Wrong. This is the trap. 'Only' flips it: counts → develops source evaluation. That makes source evaluation necessary for counting, not enough to guarantee it. The courses could meet it and still not count.
CORRECT. This is the missing link: develops source evaluation → should count. Plug it in and the chain is complete: sequence course → project → source evaluation → counts.
Wrong. A comparison between students doesn't link anything to the requirement. The conclusion's new term, counting toward info-literacy, never shows up.
Wrong. Reversed direction: counts → research project. We need research project (or source evaluation) → counts. Knowing what counting requires doesn't tell you these courses qualify.
Wrong. Courses outside the sequence are irrelevant, and this never connects to the requirement.

questions.stimulus: For decades, groundwater has been pumped heavily for irrigation in the Halden Valley, and as a result the land surface over most of the valley has sunk by more than a meter. In recent years, pumping has continued at the same rate and the water table has kept falling just as fast as before, yet the land has been sinking much more slowly than it did earlier.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: In recent years, rainfall in the Halden Valley has been greater than its long-term average.
Land sinks when the removal of groundwater allows underground layers of fine clay to compact under the weight of the material above them.
Several farms in the valley have recently switched to irrigation methods that use less water.
Most of the clay beneath the valley has already compacted nearly as far as it can, and sand barely compacts.
In a neighboring valley where far less groundwater is pumped, the land has sunk by only a few centimeters in total.
questions.explanation: The puzzle is why unchanged pumping and an equally fast-falling water table now produce less sinking. D explains it: the compressible clay has largely finished compacting, and the remaining sands barely compact. B is the tempting trap: it explains why pumping causes sinking at all but not why the sinking has slowed; A and C conflict with the stated facts that the water table and pumping rate are unchanged.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Pumping continues at the same rate and the water table is falling as fast as ever, but the land is now sinking much more slowly.

breakdown.analysis: Same cause, weaker effect. So something about the ground itself must have changed. Prephrase: the stuff that compacts has mostly already compacted. Think of squeezing a sponge: the first squeezes flatten it a lot, but once it's squashed, squeezing just as hard barely changes it.

choices.note: Wrong. Extra rain might slow the water table's fall, but the stimulus says the water table is falling just as fast as before. So rain can't be the explanation.
Wrong. The trap. It explains why pumping makes land sink at all. It doesn't explain why the sinking has slowed while pumping hasn't.
Wrong. Contradicts the facts: pumping has continued at the same rate. Even if some farms use less, the total is unchanged.
CORRECT. The clay that compacts is almost fully compacted, and what's left (sand) barely compresses. So even with the same pumping and water-table drop, there's little left to sink.
Wrong. A comparison with another valley shows that pumping causes sinking, but says nothing about why Halden's sinking slowed down.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: The Dalby Cannery cut its workers' hourly wages last month, citing recent losses. But two years ago, when the workers agreed to forgo a scheduled raise, the owners promised that wages would not be reduced so long as the cannery remained profitable over each full year. The cannery made a profit last year despite its losses in recent months. So the wage cut was unjustified.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, would most help to justify the columnist's argument?
choices: An employer that asks its workers to forgo a scheduled raise should fully explain the financial reasons behind the request.
Workers who make a concession in exchange for an employer's promise are owed that promise whenever its stated conditions are met.
Wage reductions are justified only when they are genuinely needed to keep a company from going out of business.
A company's owners may reduce wages whenever the company's monthly costs exceed its monthly revenue, regardless of its annual results.
Promises that employers make during labor negotiations are binding only if they have been put in writing.
questions.explanation: The columnist's case rests on the promise: workers gave up a raise, the promised condition (a profitable full year) held, so cutting wages broke the promise; B states exactly that principle. C is tempting, but nothing in the argument says the cut was not needed to keep the cannery open, so C could not establish the conclusion. D supports the cannery, and E would undercut the columnist unless the promise was written, which is not stated.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The cannery's wage cut was unjustified.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Two years ago workers gave up a scheduled raise; the owners promised no wage cuts as long as the cannery stayed profitable over each full year; the cannery was profitable last year.

breakdown.analysis: The argument is all about a deal: workers gave something up, the owners promised something back, and the promise's condition was met. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says. Here: if workers made a concession for a promise and the promise's conditions are met, the employer must keep it. That makes the cut unjustified. Prephrase: a promise made in exchange for a concession must be kept when its conditions hold.

choices.note: Wrong. About explaining reasons for asking workers to forgo a raise. That's not the issue. The question is whether cutting wages later was justified.

CORRECT. Workers made a concession (forgoing the raise) in exchange for a promise (no cuts while profitable for the full year), and the condition was met (profit last year). So they were owed the promise, and the cut was unjustified.
Wrong. Tempting, because it limits wage cuts. But the argument never says the cut wasn't needed to keep the cannery alive. Without that fact, C can't get you to 'unjustified.'
Wrong. Opposite. This would justify the cut, since recent months showed losses, regardless of the annual profit.
Wrong. This would hurt the columnist unless the promise was written down, which the stimulus never says. It doesn't help reach the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: After Dunmore County raised its minimum wage last year, employment at the county's restaurants did not decline. However, the average number of hours worked per restaurant employee fell by about 10 percent, and restaurants posted fewer job openings than in previous years. Over the same period, the rate at which restaurant employees quit their jobs dropped sharply.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: The increase in the minimum wage is what caused the county's restaurants to reduce the hours their employees worked.
Restaurants that reduced their employees' hours posted fewer job openings than other restaurants did.
Restaurant employees in Dunmore County earned less money in total last year than they had the year before.
The number of people employed at the county's restaurants rose after the minimum wage was increased.
Fewer employees leaving their jobs may account for part of the decline in the restaurants' job openings.
questions.explanation: Job openings arise largely when workers leave, so a sharp drop in quitting gives a plausible partial explanation for fewer openings; E's hedged claim is well supported. A is the tempting trap, but the facts show only that hours fell after the wage rose, not that the wage increase caused it. C cannot be determined without knowing how much hourly pay rose, D goes beyond 'did not decline,' and B compares restaurants the facts never distinguish.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) After the minimum wage rose, restaurant employment did not decline; 2) Average hours per employee fell about 10 percent; 3) Restaurants posted fewer job openings than in previous years; 4) The rate at which restaurant employees quit dropped sharply.

breakdown.analysis: No conclusion here, so look for the answer the facts back up without stretching. Think about where job openings come from: mostly from people leaving. If far fewer people quit, there are fewer spots to fill, so fewer openings. That's a solid, hedged inference. Be suspicious of anything claiming causation from the wage increase; the facts only give timing.

choices.note: Wrong. Tempting, but it's causal. The facts say hours fell after the wage rose, not because of it. Something else could have cut hours. Timing isn't proof.
Wrong. The facts give county-wide averages and never break restaurants into groups. This comparison has no support.
Wrong. Hours fell 10 percent, but hourly pay rose by an unknown amount. If the wage went up 20 percent, total pay could still rise. Can't be determined.
Wrong. 'Did not decline' means stayed the same or rose. You can't conclude it rose. Watch that shift.
CORRECT. The hedge ('may account for part of') makes this easy to support. Fewer people quitting means fewer vacancies to fill, which plausibly explains some of the drop in openings.

questions.stimulus: Parks official: Critics say that replacing the lawn in Orchard Square with native meadow plants was a mistake because the square now draws fewer visitors. But the meadow has cut the square's water use by 60 percent, and in a survey posted on the square's information board, 85 percent of respondents said they approve of the meadow. So the change has been popular with the public.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most undermines the parks official's defense?
choices: Several other cities in the region have replaced the lawns in their public squares with native meadow plants.
The meadow requires more frequent maintenance work by park staff than the old lawn did, which raises the square's labor costs.
Most people who stopped visiting the square after the meadow was planted did so because they preferred the lawn.
Many of the people who responded to the survey also visit other parks in the city.
Some of the survey's respondents said that they would like benches to be added along the edges of the meadow.
questions.explanation: The survey reached only people who still come to the square, so it leaves out exactly those most likely to dislike the change. C confirms that the people who stopped coming did so because they disliked the meadow, so the 85 percent figure does not reflect the public as a whole. B is the tempting trap: it supports the critics' view that the change was a mistake, but it does not touch the official's conclusion that the change is popular.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Replacing the lawn with a native meadow has been popular with the public.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The meadow cut water use by 60 percent; in a survey posted on the square's information board, 85 percent of respondents approved.

breakdown.analysis: Look at who took the survey: people standing in the square reading the board. Those are the people who still come. The people who stopped visiting, the ones most likely to hate the change, never saw it. It's like surveying diners inside a restaurant about whether they like the new menu. The water savings, by the way, are irrelevant to popularity. Prephrase: the survey's sample is biased toward people who like the meadow.

choices.note: Wrong. Other cities doing the same thing says nothing about whether Orchard Square's meadow is popular.
Wrong. The trap. Higher labor costs support the critics' claim that the change was a mistake, but the official's conclusion is about popularity. Cost doesn't touch that.

CORRECT. This confirms the bias. The people who stopped coming did so because they preferred the lawn, and they're exactly who the board survey missed. So 85 percent approval doesn't speak for the public.
Wrong. Respondents visiting other parks doesn't show they misrepresent the public's view of this meadow.
Wrong. Wanting benches added is compatible with approving of the meadow. Doesn't undermine the survey.

questions.stimulus: A utility should postpone shutting off a household's service for nonpayment whenever the household has made at least one partial payment within the past sixty days and, in addition, either someone in the household depends on electrically powered medical equipment or temperatures are forecast to fall below freezing during the following week.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: The Lees made a partial payment on their bill last month, and a hard freeze is forecast for next week, so the utility should postpone shutting off their service.
The Whitfields made a partial payment two weeks ago, and no one in the household uses medical equipment; with mild weather forecast, the utility should postpone shutting off their service.
The Garcias' last partial payment was ninety days ago, but Mr. Garcia relies on a home oxygen machine, so the utility should postpone shutting off their service.
The Novaks have made no partial payments this year, although Ms. Novak relies on a powered wheelchair, so the utility is required to shut off their service.
The Ortegas made a partial payment last month and rely on medical equipment, so the utility should both postpone their shutoff and forgive their unpaid balance.
questions.explanation: The principle requires a partial payment within sixty days plus either medical-equipment dependence or a forecast freeze. The Lees meet both parts, so A conforms. D is the subtle trap: the Novaks fail the payment condition, but the principle says only when a shutoff should be postponed, not when one is required; C fails the sixty-day condition, B meets neither of the second conditions, and E adds forgiveness, which the principle never addresses.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: If (partial payment within 60 days) AND (someone depends on powered medical equipment OR a freeze is forecast in the next week) → the utility should postpone shutoff.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the case that meets every condition and concludes only that the utility should postpone the shutoff: (1) a partial payment within the past 60 days; (2) medical-equipment dependence or a freeze forecast for the coming week.

breakdown.analysis: Two conditions, and the second is an either/or. You need the payment AND one of medical-equipment-or-freeze. Find a case that meets both and concludes 'postpone.' Note what the principle does NOT say: it never says when a shutoff is required, and never mentions forgiving debt. Failing the condition doesn't trigger the opposite.

choices.note: CORRECT. Partial payment last month (within 60 days) plus a hard freeze forecast for next week. Both parts met, so postpone.
Wrong. The payment condition is met, but neither half of the second condition is: no medical equipment and mild weather. The principle doesn't call for postponing.
Wrong. The last partial payment was 90 days ago, so the 60-day condition fails. The oxygen machine alone isn't enough.

Wrong. The subtle trap. The Novaks do fail the payment condition, but the principle only tells you when to postpone. It never says a shutoff is required otherwise. Failing a sufficient condition doesn't give you the opposite result.
Wrong. The postponement part is fine, but the principle says nothing about forgiving balances. The answer goes beyond the rule.

questions.stimulus: Every film shown at the Corvo Festival this year was chosen by the festival's selection jury, and the jury chose no film that had already been released commercially. The Long Field has already been released commercially, so it was not shown at the Corvo Festival this year.
questions.stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following arguments is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Every car sold at Henley Motors is inspected by Pratt, and Pratt inspects no car that has more than 100,000 miles on it. So the sedan Pratt inspected last week has fewer than 100,000 miles on it.
The Corbel Café's head chef prepares no dish with peanuts, and only dishes the head chef prepares appear on the café's lunch menu. The café's satay has peanuts, so it is not on that menu.

Every painting in the east gallery was donated by Ames, and Ames donated no painting that was made before 1900. The Tolland portrait was made before 1900, so it was not one of the paintings Ames donated.
Every member of the choir auditioned for the director, and the director turned away no one who could read music. Since Lin can read music, it follows that Lin must be a member of the choir.

Every book in the reading room was approved by the librarian, and the librarian approves only those books that are in good condition. This atlas is in good condition, so it must be in the reading room.
questions.explanation: The argument chains two rules (shown at the festival → chosen by the jury → not released commercially) and, from an item that lacks the final property, concludes by contrapositive that it lacks the first: it was not shown. (B) does the same with its rules stated in a different order and with 'only': the satay contains peanuts, so the chef did not prepare it, so it is not on the menu. (C) is the trap: its first sentence copies the stimulus's form, but it stops at the middle term and never uses the gallery premise. (A) reasons forward from the middle term, and (D) and (E) reverse the conditionals.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Long Field was not shown at the Corvo Festival this year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every film shown was chosen by the jury; the jury chose no film already released commercially; The Long Field was already released commercially.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: A → B; B → not C; this item is C; so it is not B, and so not A.

breakdown.analysis: Diagram it. Shown → chosen by jury → not released. The Long Field is released, so by contrapositive: not chosen, and so not shown. The conclusion lands on the FIRST term of the chain. Find the answer that runs the whole chain backward to the first term. Most students pick (C) because its first sentence is a carbon copy: 'Every … was … by Ames, and Ames … no …'. It fails because it concludes only that Ames didn't donate the portrait. That's the middle term; the gallery premise does no work. Like proving a dish wasn't cooked by the chef and stopping there, never saying it's not on the menu. (B) hides because it puts the second rule first and phrases the first one with 'only': only chef-prepared dishes are on the menu means on menu → chef prepared.

choices.note: Wrong. This starts from the middle term (Pratt inspected it) and runs forward to a conclusion. It never uses the Henley premise and never denies anything by contrapositive.

CORRECT. On menu → chef prepared ('only'); chef prepared → no peanuts. The satay has peanuts, so the chef didn't prepare it, so it's not on the menu. Same two-step contrapositive back to the first term.

Tempting. It looks the most like the stimulus. But it stops halfway: not donated by Ames. It never concludes the portrait isn't in the east gallery, so the first premise is idle. Half the chain is not the same pattern.
Wrong. 'Turned away no one who could read music' doesn't mean everyone who reads music joined. It reverses the conditional: from the condition to membership.
Wrong. Reading room → good condition. Being in good condition doesn't put the atlas in the reading room. Reversed conditional.

questions.stimulus: Some historians argue that the Brennock Canal was built mainly to carry coal, pointing out that coal made up most of its cargo in the decades after it opened. But the canal company's charter, drafted before the region's large coal seams had been discovered, names only grain and timber as the cargo the canal was meant to serve. The coal traffic, then, reflects a use that arose later, and it reveals little about why the canal was built.
questions.stem: The claim that coal made up most of the canal's cargo in the decades after it opened plays which one of the following roles in the argument?
choices: It is a claim that the argument tries to show is false, using evidence drawn from the canal company's charter.
It is a premise that the argument uses, together with the charter's contents, to establish the builders' actual purpose.
It is the main conclusion of an argument that the author contends rests on a misreading of the charter.
It is offered as evidence that the canal's builders did not foresee the discovery of coal.
Others cite it to support a view that the argument rejects, and the argument grants its truth.
questions.explanation: The historians cite the coal traffic as evidence that the canal was built for coal. The author accepts that coal dominated the cargo but argues, from the charter, that this reflects a later use and reveals little about why the canal was built. So the claim is others' evidence for a rejected view, and its truth is granted: (E). (A) is the trap: the author rejects the historians' conclusion, not the fact they rely on. (B) misassigns the support, (C) confuses the historians' evidence with their conclusion, and (D) has no basis.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The coal traffic reflects a later use and reveals little about why the Brennock Canal was built.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The charter, written before the coal seams were found, names only grain and timber; some historians cite the coal cargo as proof the canal was built for coal.

breakdown.analysis: Who says coal made up most of the cargo? The historians, and the author never argues with it. The author's fight is over what the coal traffic shows: a later use, not the original purpose. So the claim is a fact the author grants but says doesn't support the historians' conclusion. Most students pick (A) because the author is clearly disagreeing with the historians, and the claim belongs to the historians. It fails because the author disputes their conclusion, not this fact; 'The coal traffic, then, reflects a use that arose later' takes the coal traffic as real. It's like conceding your rival scored the most points this season but denying that makes them the best defender. (E) hides behind an abstract stand-in, 'a view that the argument rejects.'

choices.note: Tempting. The author does oppose the historians. But the author never says coal wasn't most of the cargo. The charter is used to show what the canal was originally for, not to deny the coal traffic.
Wrong. The charter alone shows the builders' purpose. The coal claim doesn't help establish that purpose; the author says it reveals little about it.

Wrong. The coal claim is the historians' evidence, not their conclusion. Their conclusion is that the canal was built mainly to carry coal. And the author's complaint isn't that they misread the charter.
Wrong. Nothing uses the coal cargo to show what the builders anticipated. The charter's timing does that work, not the cargo.
CORRECT. The historians offer it to support their view; the author rejects that view but accepts the fact, arguing only that it reflects a later use.

questions.stimulus: Records show that the silent film The Lantern Keeper was shown in only three cities during its original release, and few reviews of it were published. Yet its distinctive camera techniques appear in dozens of films by directors who began working in the years just after its release. These directors, then, must have seen The Lantern Keeper.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: At least some of the directors who used the techniques lived in or visited one of the three cities during the film's original release.
The few reviews of The Lantern Keeper that were published at the time singled out its camera techniques for praise.
The directors who used the techniques were, on the whole, more innovative than most other directors working at the time.
None of the directors who used the techniques acquired them solely by studying the films of other directors who used them.
The Lantern Keeper was seen by more people than the surviving records of its original release indicate.
questions.explanation: The argument infers that every director who used the techniques must have seen the film, which requires that the techniques could not reach them by another route. Dozens of films used them, so a later director could have picked them up from an earlier imitator. Negate (D): some director learned the techniques only from other directors' films, and that director need not have seen The Lantern Keeper. (A) is the trap: it looks like a modest access assumption, but the argument never says the directors saw the film during its original release, so they could have seen it later. (E), (B), and (C) are not required.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The directors whose films use The Lantern Keeper's camera techniques must have seen The Lantern Keeper.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The film showed in only three cities in its original release and got few reviews; its distinctive techniques appear in dozens of films by directors who started soon after.

breakdown.analysis: 'Must have seen' is very strong. It takes for granted that using the techniques means you saw the original. But dozens of films used them. Couldn't a director have copied the techniques from one of those other films? Like a cover band learning a song from another cover band, never hearing the original. We need an answer that rules out second-hand learning. Most students pick (A) because it looks like the classic hedged NA answer about access to the film. It fails because the argument never says the directors saw the film during its original release; the three-city limit applies only to that run, and they could have seen it later. (D) hides because it's about other directors' films, which the stimulus never mentions, and because it's worded strongly ('none'). It has to be: the conclusion covers every one of 'these directors.'

choices.note: Tempting. 'At least some' sounds like a safe necessary assumption. But the directors could have seen the film after its original release, at a later screening or from a print. Negate it and the argument survives.
choices.negation: None of the directors who used the techniques lived in or visited one of the three cities during the film's original release.

choices.note: Wrong. What reviewers praised doesn't matter. The directors could have seen the film no matter what the reviews said. Negating it does no damage.
choices.negation: The few reviews published at the time did not all single out the film's camera techniques for praise.

choices.note: Wrong. How innovative the directors were is beside the point. Negating it changes nothing about whether they saw the film.
choices.negation: The directors who used the techniques were not, on the whole, more innovative than most other directors of the time.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: some director learned the techniques only from imitators' films. That director needn't have seen The Lantern Keeper, so 'these directors must have seen it' fails.
choices.negation: At least one of the directors who used the techniques acquired them solely by studying the films of other directors who used them.

choices.note: Wrong. It would help, but it isn't required. Even if the records are accurate, the directors could be among the people who saw the film. Negating it doesn't break the argument.
choices.negation: The Lantern Keeper was not seen by more people than the surviving records of its original release indicate.

questions.stimulus: Conservationist: Any bird species in the Pellam Islands whose nests are within reach of the introduced rats is in danger of local extinction unless it breeds more than once a year. Every bird species in danger of local extinction there should be included in the new captive-breeding program. The Pellam rail nests only on the ground, where the rats can reach its nests. So the Pellam rail should be included in the captive-breeding program.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the conservationist's argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Only bird species whose nests are within reach of the rats should be included in the new captive-breeding program.
The Pellam rail breeds less often than any other bird species in the Pellam Islands whose nests the rats can reach.
Any bird species that breeds only once a year is in danger of local extinction if rats can reach its nests.
Every bird species in the Pellam Islands that nests only on the ground breeds more than once a year.
Pellam bird species that breed more than once a year all nest at least partly off the ground.
questions.explanation: The rail's nests are within the rats' reach, so it is in danger, and belongs in the program, unless it breeds more than once a year; the argument needs to rule that out. (E), by contrapositive, says a species that nests only on the ground does not breed more than once a year, which completes the chain. (B) is the trap: breeding less often than every other exposed species is a relative claim and is compatible with breeding twice a year. (C) restates part of the first rule, (A) is irrelevant, and (D) would defeat the conclusion.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Pellam rail should be included in the captive-breeding program.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Nests within rats' reach AND not breeding more than once a year → in danger; in danger → should be in the program; the rail nests only on the ground, within the rats' reach.

breakdown.analysis: Build the chain. Rats can reach the nests → in danger UNLESS the species breeds more than once a year. In danger → program. We know the rail's nests are reachable. What's missing? That the rail does NOT breed more than once a year. Find the answer that guarantees it. (E) does it in contrapositive form: breeds more than once a year → nests at least partly off the ground. Contrapositive: nests only on the ground → doesn't breed more than once a year. The rail nests only on the ground. Done. Most students pick (B) because 'breeds less often than any other' sounds like 'breeds rarely.' It fails because it's relative. If every other exposed species breeds three times a year, the rail could breed twice and escape the danger rule. Watch the switch from a relative word (less often) to an absolute one (not more than once).

choices.note: Wrong. This limits who else can be included. It says nothing about whether the rail breeds more than once a year, which is the missing link.

Tempting. It sounds like the rail barely breeds. But 'less often than the others' is relative. The rail could still breed twice a year if the others breed more, and then the danger rule doesn't apply.
Wrong. This restates part of the first rule. It doesn't tell you how often the rail breeds, so the chain still has a gap.
Wrong. Opposite. If ground-only nesters breed more than once a year, the rail escapes the danger rule and the conclusion doesn't follow.
CORRECT. Contrapositive: nests only on the ground → does not breed more than once a year. The rail nests only on the ground, so it's in danger and belongs in the program.

questions.stimulus: A Quarrow apple seedling will bear fruit in its third year only if it has been grafted onto dwarf rootstock and is planted where it gets full sun. Every seedling in Mira Okonjo's new orchard row was grafted onto dwarf rootstock, and the row faces south with no shade at all. So the seedlings in that row will bear fruit in their third year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: Any tenant at the Hesketh Building who gives sixty days' notice and leaves the unit undamaged gets the full deposit back. The Wrexleys gave sixty days' notice and left their unit undamaged, so they will get their full security deposit back.

Any runner who finishes the qualifying race in under three hours and has paid the entry fee will be admitted to the championship. Dana paid the fee but finished in over three hours, so she will not be admitted to the championship.

A volunteer may handle the rare maps in the city archive only if she has completed conservation training and been approved by the curator. Petra has not been approved by the curator, so she may not handle the rare maps.

No orchestra will be considered for the festival's opening night unless it has played at the festival before and has a board-approved conductor. The Tamberly Orchestra has played there twice and has such a conductor, so it will be considered.

Each of the four members of the Pindar Quartet is an accomplished soloist who has won national competitions. So the Pindar Quartet must itself be an accomplished ensemble, one that would win national competitions for quartets.
questions.explanation: Grafting and full sun are stated as necessary conditions for third-year fruit ('only if'), but the argument treats meeting them as enough to guarantee fruit. (D) makes the same error: 'unless' makes past play and an approved conductor necessary for consideration, and the orchestra meeting both is taken to guarantee it. (A) is the trap: it also shows two conditions met and draws the conclusion, but its conditions are sufficient ('any tenant who … gets'), so it is valid. (C) validly denies a necessary condition, (B) wrongly negates a sufficient condition, and (E) moves from parts to the whole.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The seedlings in Okonjo's row will bear fruit in their third year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Third-year fruit → dwarf rootstock AND full sun; the row's seedlings have dwarf rootstock and full sun.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: X only if A and B; this case has A and B; so X. (Necessary conditions treated as sufficient.)

breakdown.analysis: 'Only if' introduces what's required, not what's enough. Fruit → rootstock and sun. Having rootstock and sun doesn't get you fruit: the seedlings could still need water, pollination, a mild winter. It's like saying you can only pass the bar if you go to law school, so everyone who went to law school passed. Find the answer that meets every NECESSARY condition and then concludes the outcome. Most students pick (A) because it looks identical on the surface: two conditions, both met, conclusion follows. It fails because (A)'s conditions are sufficient: 'any tenant who gives sixty days' notice and leaves the unit undamaged gets the full deposit back.' Meeting a sufficient condition does guarantee the result, so (A) is valid, and a valid argument can't share a flaw. (D) hides behind 'unless': 'No orchestra will be considered unless A and B' means considered → A and B. Same necessary conditions, same illegal leap.

choices.note: Tempting. Two conditions met, conclusion drawn: it looks like a twin of the stimulus. But here the conditions are sufficient: any tenant who does both gets the deposit back. The Wrexleys did both, so the conclusion follows. Valid, so not the same flaw.

Wrong. A different error. Finishing under three hours plus paying is sufficient for admission; failing one part doesn't prove Dana won't be admitted some other way. That's negating a sufficient condition, not treating a necessary one as sufficient.
Wrong. Valid. Curator approval is necessary for handling the maps, and Petra lacks it, so she may not handle them. Denying a necessary condition is the right way to use one.

CORRECT. 'Unless' marks necessary conditions: considered → played before AND approved conductor. The Tamberly Orchestra meets both, and the argument concludes it will be considered. Necessary taken as sufficient, just like the orchard.
Wrong. A different flaw: part to whole. Great soloists needn't make a great quartet. No conditional is involved.

questions.stimulus: Granite boulders scattered across the Tamsin Plain are of a type found in place only in the Dovre Mountains, 200 kilometers to the north. Geologists know of only two processes able to carry boulders that far: glaciers and catastrophic floods. Boulders carried by floods are rounded and smoothed, whereas boulders carried by glaciers typically keep sharp edges and often bear parallel scratches. Most of the Dovre granite boulders on the plain have sharp edges, though a few are rounded.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: The rounded boulders on the Tamsin Plain were carried there by catastrophic floods.
All of the Dovre granite boulders on the Tamsin Plain were carried there by a single glacier.
At least some of the Dovre granite boulders on the Tamsin Plain were carried there by glaciers.
Most of the Dovre granite boulders on the Tamsin Plain bear parallel scratches.
No catastrophic flood has ever swept from the Dovre Mountains to the Tamsin Plain.
questions.explanation: Flood-carried boulders are rounded, so the many sharp-edged boulders could not have come by flood; since only glaciers and floods could carry them, those boulders were carried by glaciers, as C says. A is the tempting trap: glacier-carried boulders only 'typically' keep sharp edges, so the few rounded ones could also have arrived by glacier. B and E ignore the rounded boulders' uncertain origin, and D overstates 'often bear' scratches.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1) Granite boulders on the Tamsin Plain come only from the Dovre Mountains, 200 km away; 2) Only glaciers and catastrophic floods can carry boulders that far; 3) Flood-carried boulders are rounded and smoothed; 4) Glacier-carried boulders typically keep sharp edges and often have parallel scratches; 5) Most of the plain's boulders are sharp-edged; a few are rounded.

breakdown.analysis: Use the strict rule, not the loose one. Floods → rounded. Contrapositive: sharp-edged → not carried by flood. Only two options exist, so sharp-edged → glacier. Most boulders are sharp, so at least some (in fact most) came by glacier. The rounded ones are a mystery: glacier boulders only 'typically' stay sharp, so a rounded one could have come either way.

choices.note: Wrong. The trap. Floods → rounded doesn't give you rounded → flood. Glacier boulders only 'typically' keep sharp edges, so some rounded ones might have come by glacier too.
Wrong. Too strong twice over. The rounded boulders could have come by flood, and nothing says only one glacier was involved.
CORRECT. Floods always round boulders, so the sharp-edged ones didn't come by flood. With only two possible carriers, they came by glacier. 'At least some' is easily supported.
Wrong. Glacier boulders 'often' bear scratches, not usually. You can't get to 'most' from 'often.'
Wrong. The rounded boulders may well have come by flood. Nothing rules a flood out.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Two years after the town of Ashby began requiring employers to list salary ranges in job postings, the gap between the average starting salaries of men and women hired by Ashby firms had narrowed considerably. The requirement probably narrowed the gap by giving applicants, many of whom had previously had little idea what a position paid, a firmer basis for negotiating their pay.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the economist's argument?
choices: Before the requirement took effect, surveys found that many job applicants in Ashby had little idea what the positions they sought paid.
Some Ashby employers had already been listing salary ranges in their job postings before the requirement took effect.
Job postings in Ashby that list salary ranges tend to attract more applicants than do postings that do not list them.
Women hired by Ashby firms since the requirement took effect have, on average, more work experience than women hired before it.
The gap narrowed mostly in jobs with negotiated starting pay and hardly at all in jobs with fixed pay scales.
questions.explanation: The economist claims both that the requirement narrowed the gap and that it did so by aiding negotiation. (E) fits that mechanism: the gap shrank where pay is negotiated and not where it is fixed, which is hard to explain unless the change worked through negotiation. (A) is the trap: it confirms that applicants lacked pay information, but the economist already states that, so it adds no support for the causal claim. (D) offers an alternative cause, (B) if anything slightly weakens, and (C) is irrelevant to the gap.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ashby's salary-range requirement probably narrowed the gender gap in starting salaries by giving applicants a firmer basis for negotiating.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Two years after the requirement, the gap between men's and women's average starting salaries had narrowed considerably; many applicants had previously had little idea what jobs paid.

breakdown.analysis: The gap narrowed after the rule. Was it the rule, and was it through negotiation? Lots of things could narrow a pay gap: who got hired, which jobs grew, general trends. The best support would show the change happened exactly where the proposed mechanism works. If negotiation is the channel, the gap should shrink where pay is negotiated and not where it's fixed. Most students pick (A) because it lines up with the economist's story. It fails because it only repeats a fact the economist already gave you: applicants used to lack pay information. Confirming a premise is irrelevant corroboration; it doesn't make the causal link any more likely. (E) hides because it never mentions the requirement or women; it just tells you where the narrowing happened.

choices.note: Tempting. It sounds like evidence for the economist. But the stimulus already says many applicants had little idea what positions paid. Repeating a given premise adds nothing to the case that the requirement caused the narrowing.
Wrong. If some employers already listed ranges, the requirement changed less than it seems. If anything that slightly weakens the argument.
Wrong. More applicants per posting says nothing about whether men's and women's pay converged, or why.
Wrong. This is an alternative cause: more experienced women would earn more regardless of the requirement. It weakens.

CORRECT. The narrowing tracks the proposed mechanism: big where pay is bargained, near zero where it's fixed. A general trend wouldn't split that way, so this supports both that the rule worked and how.

questions.stimulus: Library board member: Advocates of eliminating overdue fines at Corland's public libraries claim that doing so would increase the number of books borrowed, and they cite a pilot program at the Wexley branch, where borrowing rose after fines were dropped. But the pilot coincided with the opening of a large school next door to the Wexley branch, which by itself could have increased borrowing there. So eliminating overdue fines would not increase the number of books borrowed.
questions.stem: The board member's reasoning is flawed in that it
choices: attacks the motives of those who advocate eliminating overdue fines rather than addressing the evidence that they cite
fails to establish that the opening of the school actually caused borrowing at the Wexley branch to rise
presumes that an increase in borrowing is the only reason anyone has offered for eliminating overdue fines
overlooks the possibility that ending fines could raise borrowing even if the school explains Wexley's rise
takes for granted that results from a pilot program at a single branch cannot show anything about a citywide policy
questions.explanation: The board member legitimately shows that the Wexley pilot does not establish its conclusion, since the new school is an uncontrolled alternative cause, but then concludes that eliminating fines would not increase borrowing. Undercutting the evidence for a claim does not show the claim false: ending fines could still raise borrowing, which is (D). (B) is the trap: offering a possible alternative explanation is enough to undercut the pilot as evidence, so the member need not prove the school caused the rise. (C) and (E) describe reasoning the member never uses, and (A) misdescribes an argument that addresses the evidence directly.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Eliminating overdue fines would not increase the number of books borrowed.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Advocates cite the Wexley pilot, where borrowing rose after fines were dropped; a large school opened next door during the pilot and could by itself explain the rise.

breakdown.analysis: The board member does a fine job of poking a hole in the pilot: the school is a confound. That's enough to say 'the pilot doesn't prove anything.' But the conclusion goes further: eliminating fines would NOT increase borrowing. Bad evidence for a claim isn't good evidence against it. It's like: your only witness was drunk, so the crime never happened. Most students pick (B) because the member only says the school 'could have' raised borrowing, and that sounds like an unproven claim. It fails because a possible alternative cause is all you need to undercut the pilot; that part of the argument is fine. The mistake is the leap from 'unproven' to 'false.' (D) hides in omission form: it describes the case the member ignores rather than naming the flaw.

choices.note: Wrong. The board member doesn't mention the advocates' motives at all. The argument engages the evidence directly.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The advocates want fines eliminated only because they have overdue books themselves, so their argument should be ignored.

choices.note: Tempting. The member only says the school could have raised borrowing. But that's enough to show the pilot doesn't prove the advocates' claim. To undercut evidence, a plausible alternative cause is sufficient. The flaw is what the member concludes after that.
Wrong. The argument is about borrowing only. It presumes nothing about other reasons for eliminating fines, and its conclusion doesn't depend on them.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Eliminating fines won't raise borrowing, so there's no reason at all to eliminate them.

choices.note: CORRECT. Even if the school explains the Wexley rise, ending fines might still raise borrowing. The member treats the pilot's failure as proof of the opposite, which doesn't follow.
Wrong. The member's objection is a specific confound at Wexley, not that one branch can never tell us anything. This misdescribes the reasoning.
choices.example: Example of flaw: One branch is too small to tell us anything, so the pilot is worthless regardless of how it was run.
